subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of the Canadian House of Commons my first words this afternoon should be those of sympathy with hon. members of the House of Commons of the mother of parliaments in the destruction of her Commons chamber on Friday night at the hands of Hitler's airmen. In a very real sense, not only to those of us whose ancestors came from the British isles, and who were living there when those shrines of empire were built-the House of Commons, Westminster Abbey and Westminster Hall-but to all peoples who have espoused democracy as their form of government, the destruction of the commons chamber of the mother of parliaments is symbolical of what the forces of totalitarianism would do with our whole democratic system if only once they obtained power to do it.
No shrine-nothing-is sacred to those people, or will be permitted to stand in the way of their desire to dominate the world. As one thinks of what the people in England are enduring to-day, and as he reads about the bombings of hospitals filled with patients, among whom are little children, he considers what it must mean when a hospital is bombed in the middle of the night and children are maimed and killed. It makes people in this country feel that they should rededicate themselves to the task of saving England from defeat, of upholding her hands; for there can be very little doubt that if the front line of freedom goes down in the British isles, that front line will move to this side of the Atlantic, and what the women and children of England are enduring to-day, the women and children of Montreal and Toronto and Ottawa will have to endure in their turn. I well remember three years ago when we read of the bombing of the women and children of China. At that time we were inclined to feel that that would never happen to English-speaking women and children. We did not realize then that the fight against the democracies had already started. At that time there were those in this parliament who doubted the wisdom of our preparing even in a modest way to defend ourselves. Apparently some of them seem even now, when the war has spread over practically the whole of the earth's surface with the exception of the Americas, to think that we can still sit back and let Great Britain go down without dire results to ourselves. As I said, I want, my first word to

be an expression of sympathy to our brother commoners in the British isles and an expression of our deep determination to stay with them through these dark days until the sun of victory again shines upon the banners of the democracies of the world.
In case I should forget, may I say now that I am speaking upon the motion to go into committee of ways and means and the amendments which have been moved thereto by a member of the Social Credit group and a member of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I do not intend to read these amendments. I realize that an amendment of this kind may contain many desirable things; I realize that in such an amendment one could include statements or expressions that would be opposed by no one in this house. But simply because an amendment contains something with which we may be sympathetic does not mean that we should vote for it. In the committee of ways and means the government submits for consideration the specific proposals by which it intends to raise money to carry on this struggle. If the motion for committee of ways and means does not carry; if these amendments, which are really votes of want of confidence in the government, should carry, at the very most it would mean an election, and at the very least it would mean an indication that in this house there are those who would deny this request to have money voted with which to carry on the war. I should like to compliment the official opposition upon the attitude it has taken in refusing to stand in the way of that request by moving an amendment. I think they have shown the right attitude. I quite realize that in time of peace such tactics are part of the ways of democracy, but in a time like this the advice given by Prime Minister Menzies should be taken to heart by every hon. member of this House of Commons, and anything which stands in the way of these war proposals should find no place here at this time.
I was interested to note that after the debate in the House of Commons in Great Britain following the speech of Prime Minister Churchill, Mr. Lloyd George, who had been critical of what the British government had done, abstained from voting. The newspapers circulating in Germany and in the enemy occupied countries did not note the fact that only three men had voted against that motion; they circulated the fact that the great wartime Prime Minister of Great Britain had abstained from voting. They were indicating to the people that there must be a considerable proportion of the people of Great Britain who were not solidly behind Churchill in this time of trial and testing of the British people.

The Budget-Mr. Tucker
Similarly, if any substantial part of this house voted against the granting of supply to carry on this war, undoubtedly it would be used in Germany and Italy to show that the people of this country are not unitedly behind our war effort. I do not care what is put in any amendment, I do not care what fine sentiments it may contain, if it means the denying to the government which is our agent the means of carrying on this struggle, I would have no difficulty in deciding to vote against such an amendment and uphold the duly elected government of my country.
It might be said, and I know it has been said that those who opposed the government of Chamberlain and finally brought into office the government of Churchill actually did a good jot) for England. It might be thought by some that by opposing the government at this time they would be following the lead of those who opposed the government of Mr. Chamberlain.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It might not be a bad idea.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I propose to deal with that for a few minutes this afternoon. The situation is different, for many reasons. In the first place this government has been recently returned by the people. The people have expressed their desire, as I see it, not so much in connection with the particular policies which were laid before them at the time of the election, but rather to indicate the men whom they wanted to lead them through this crisis. The people were not deciding upon any particular policies, because in time of war you cannot be sure what policy it may be necessary to follow as the type of the conflict changes; they were deciding that they would rather have the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) as their leaders at this time.
That having been decided a little over a year ago, what conceivable purpose can be served now by moving an amendment which shows lack of confidence in a government which has been newly elected by the people? What purpose can be served except to break up the unity of our people when unity is allimportant? I think that is something we should keep in mind at all times, that unity among ourselves at this time is all-important. We are in the nature of an army which is fighting for its very existence. No army can succeed if it is being torn continually by division and doubts as to the wisdom of the policies being followed or the commands being given. I, for one, believe that it is much better to unite solidly behind a leadership which may not always be absolutely perfect than continually to debate and wrangle and
weaken ourselves by trying to adopt what one individual or another thinks would be better or more nearly perfect.
My attitude has been and will be that the purpose of this House of Commons should not be to give a lead to people who are trying to weaken this government throughout the country. We should not provide arguments by which that government can be struck down, by which disunity can be created, by which cleavages may be brought about between different races and different religions.
On the contrary, we should give leadership in unity, leadership in forming a solid group behind the government. I grant that there should be criticism, but it should be constructive criticism. I grant that suggestions should be offered, but amendments should not be moved which show that there is not confidence in the duly elected government of our country.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That would apply also to some of the members of the government.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have a certain line of
argument which I want to follow. When I am finished, if the hon. member wants to ask me some questions or find fault with my speech, he will be quite welcome to do so.
I have in mind the attitude adopted by the great leader of the republican party in the recent election in the United States. Mr. Willkie fought very hard to defeat the president of the United States, but once the election was over he took the stand:	Mr. Roosevelt is my president.
There were little Republicans in the United States who were concerned about the political fortunes of their party and who found fault with that attitude of Mr. Willkie, and Mr. Willkie was immediately repudiated by some of them because he was not putting his party above his country. I saw an editorial not long ago in one of our newspapers, published not very far from this building, asking why it was that we did not get the same inspired leadership in Canada that is given by leaders like Mr. Churchill and Mr. Roosevelt, Mr. Menzies and so on. In the first place, Mr. Speaker, a prophet is not without honour save in his own home, and I have no doubt that if our Prime Minister were to go to Australia, going as he would with a message of encouragement to the people of Australia, his message would have just as good an effect upon them, I have no doubt, as that of Mr. Menzies had upon us. In the next place, there are these little Republicans in the United States who decry Mr. Roosevelt and say that he is not a great leader. Indeed, some of them say they would just about as soon have Hitler as
The Budget-Mr. Tucker

Roosevelt. We do not feel that way here, and when Mr. Roosevelt comes to Canada we shall welcome him and regard him as the great leader of our neighbours to the south.
Our own leaders are doing a good job. Everybody is entitled to his own opinion in a democracy, and in my opinion the government of this country is doing a good job. Probably the best job is being done in the field of external affairs by the Prime Minister himself. The work that he has done in bringing together the United States, Canada and the rest of the British commonwealth cannot be told now. It will be known only when the secret documents which have passed between the leaders of the various governments of the United States, Great Britain and Canada can be made public after this war is over. But I make this prediction, that long after the criticism of little errors and little mistakes is forgotten, when historians with all the facts before them come to write the story of this war, the struggle of the democracies to defend themselves, and the gathering-together into one camp of all the English-speaking nations and all the forces of free democracies the world over, it will record that while Mr. Churchill gave inspired, courageous and indomitable leadership to the peoples of the British commonwealth, he had an able lieutenant in the person of the Prime Minister of Canada who acted as a bridge between the United States and the British commonwealth in its hour of trial and ultimately brought the two nations together and thereby made ultimate triumph certain.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that I believed it was fair and proper that the members of this House of Commons should make any suggestions which they thought would be helpful. I think we all want to play some part in helping to won this war, and the government should welcome suggestions from members of the house no matter from which party they come, so long as they are made in a spirit of constructive criticism, and not with any idea of trying to divide the people or to gain party advantage. It is my definite opinion that not enough use is being made of the members of this house.
One of the things about which I feel very strongly is this. There is no doubt that one of the most fundamentally vital questions in regard to the successful cariying on of this war is: how you are going to manage your fiscal policy, your taxation policy, your monetary policy. What is the situation to-day?
I have every confidence in the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). He is a very able minister. I think, too, that those in charge of the Bank of Canada and the officials of the finance department are very able gentlemen.
[Mr. Tucker.l
The more I have come to know them the more I have come to respect them for their ability. But to turn the entire control over the country's monetary and financial policy to a group of men, no matter how able- and after all that is what it means, if the House of Commons is not called upon to check it up in any way through the banking and commerce committee-is an entirely different matter. It is impossible for the minister himself to consider all suggestions from all angles as they could be considered by the banking and commerce committee or some smaller committee perhaps that might be set up, where these suggestions could be gone into thoroughly with the able officials of the department and where we could consider them together. If the government takes the attitude that that should not be done, it simply means that the government-I say this again, as I repeated it in my last speech-is showing more confidence in the permanent officials than it has in the elected representatives of the people. We are fighting in this war this very thing of putting certain people in charge of some activity because they are probably the best men that can be found to handle it and then allowing them to be dictators. It is true that his officials must advise the minister, but as I say, he alone does not and cannot expect to be able to speak for all the members of the whole House of Commons unless their opinions and advice also are ascertained.
I earnestly submit that the report of the Bank of Canada, which after all shows what has been done on behalf of the people by that great agency of government which is becoming more and more important, should without question be referred to the banking and commerce committee for study arid suggestions. I think, too, that other important suggestions that might be made should be so referred.
As an example of what I mean: I asked a question in this house as to the extent to which Great Britain is financing her war effort at the present time on a short-term basis and therefore on a very cheap basis. Great Britain is raising far more money on a short-term basis than she is on a long-term basis, using the banks and other institutions for that purpose, without putting too heavy a burden, comparatively speaking, upon the people. I do not wish to go into the matter at any length at this moment. I cannot do it. But there are members of this House of Commons, perhaps not as well trained as the head of the Bank of Canada or the head of the finance department, who have ideas and who were elected by the people to -help determine the policy of this country, and surely they are

The Budget-Mr. Tucker
entitled to consider the policy that is being decided upon and to discuss it and help the minister in determining what the right policy in this regard should be. I do not think there can be any doubt about that being a sound attitude to take-that the House of Commons should be used in every way possible to achieve the maximum effort at this time.
I have mentioned one matter. I will give another example. Mr. Keynes is recognized as one of the most outstanding economists in the whole world to-day. He has been called in by the British government to advise it as to the financing of its war effort. One of his suggestions is that part of the heavy taxation levied on people in the lower income brackets be credited to them and repaid over a period of time after the war is over. The poorer people of the country do not mind so much paying heavier taxation in a time of trial like this, knowing that when the war is over and the period of readjustment comes they will have some of their money back to tide them over that period. In my opinion this is a splendid idea; it is something which we could discuss with the permanent departmental officials, and we might well get the opinion of Mr. Keynes as to its applicability to conditions in Canada. Surely it cannot be supposed by the permanent officials or by the minister himself that within their group is contained all knowledge, all possible helpful suggestions and ideas, and that hon. members who constitute the banking and commerce committee of this house can give them no help. If, then, they admit that there may be some members of that committee who could afford assistance in this critical time, surely, instead of its being kept here and given no opportunity of helping to decide financial policies, the committee should be called together and given the chance to do its part.
Another matter I should like to mention is that of wheat storage. In that direction, too, the members of this house should be given a chance to do something worth while. We know that to carry wheat at the present storage rates will cost about $50,000,000 a year. If we are going to be able to take from the farmers no more than 230 million bushels a year, that means that the farmer will receive roughly about $115 million, and on the other hand the people who store his grain will get nearly half that amount, or $50 million. Such an arrangement, I am convinced, will not in the long run satisfy the people of this country. Various solutions have been proposed on the floor of this house. For instance, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) has advocated that we take over the whole storage handling system. That course is objected to by some. It was
suggested by some of us two years ago that storage charges on wheat be reduced to half a cent a bushel per month; as a matter of fact they were then cut to two-thirds of a cent, but I think that the figure should be further reduced. Some may argue that this does not provide the owners of storage facilities with a fair return on their investment. Well, the committee on agriculture and colonization has upon it some of the ablest men in this house: why should it not be called together to study the problem, hear representations from all interested parties, and attempt to work out some scheme which will commend itself to the fair judgment of this country and of this house?
We are not sent here-God forbid-in this time of crisis merely to sit in this house and debate, without getting our teeth into some of these problems and helping the government to carry on. As a loyal supporter of the government, as one who always had and still has every confidence in its leadership, I ask the government to give the members of this house a chance to help them carry the burdens which they are carrying to-day. If they do so they will find greater satisfaction, not only among the members of this house, but throughout the length and breadth of the country.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I had in mind mainly
the consideration that at this time we do look to the government for leadership. An example I have in mind is with regard to the report of the Bank of Canada. H for some reason the government does not want the banking and commerce committee to meet; if in its judgment such a proceeding would be a weak-
The Budget-Mr. Tucker

ness to the war effort of the country, or in any way unhelpful, so far as I am concerned there is nothing more to be said. I have just thrown out the suggestion to the government; if for conclusive reasons it is not accepted, well and good. I am not going to embarrass the government by making a motion or anything of the sort. I realize that what the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has said is correct. I am not blaming him at all; my suggestion was made not in any spirit of carping criticism, but rather from the motive of desiring that every possible helpful agency be set to work at this time.
Another matter, with which I wish to deal very briefly, is the position of agriculture in western Canada. I intended to go into the subject at considerable length, but I see that time, as usual, has passed faster than I expected.
As a preliminary to what I intended to say, I should like to refer hon. members to a speech of the Hon. W. R. Motherwell in this chamber in the session of 1938. He pointed out, as reported in Hansard, page 4452, that in the last war, when wheat was scarce, the government stepped in and kept the price down. He quoted the following from the evidence given by Doctor Magill before the agriculture committee of the House of Commons in 1922:
We had no information about the British buying, and I stated that if the United States and Great Britain were going to compete in our markets for our hard red fife it would not surprise me to see our wheat anywhere from $3 to $5 per bushel.
Actually wheat on the open market did go up to, I believe, $4 a bushel. The average price to the farmers during these years was S2.28 a bushel, and Doctor Motherwell gave it as his opinion that by virtue of that pricefixing policy the farmers of western Canada- I would like everybody to bear this in mind- were deprived during the last war of probably between $500 and $600 million. Now, when it comes to the point, in this war, where their product is not needed, we should remember, I submit, what was done to them when their product was very much in demand and then they were quite willing to have the price fixed and kept down in order to contribute to the common effort.
Of all these people in western Canada, those who have been most hardly hit are the farmers of Saskatchewan. We know, of course, that all over Canada the agriculturists have been hit, but the wheat growers have been affected most because of the loss of a great part of their markets. Consider the index of the purchasing power of the western grain grower. In 1925 it was 104 as compared with 100 in 1913; in 1926 it stood at 88; in 1927 at 100. At that

time the purchasing power of an acre sowed to wheat was practically the same as in 1913. In 1940 the purchasing power of an acre of wheat is only 54-4. As I have said, Saskatchewan is hurt more than any other part of the west because a larger part of its income is derived from the production of wheat.
Taking the farm revenue of the three prairie provinces in 1940, only 33-2 per cent of the income of the farmer in Manitoba came from wheat; in Saskatchewan it was 70 per cent and in Alberta 47 per cent. One can see therefore that any policy that cuts down the wheat acreage necessarily hurts Saskatchewan more than its does either of the other two provinces. There is no doubt that this policy of cutting down the acreage hits us a good deal harder than the amount voted for acreage reduction helps us. Assuming that last year we had 470 million bushels of wheat to deliver in western Canada, that ^would give us $235,000,000; this year we are permitted to deliver only 230 million bushels and that cuts the income from wheat down to $115,000,000, or a reduction of $120,000,000 for the people of western Canada, who are already on a very low standard of living.
It is true that $35,000,000 is voted to help deal with that situation, but it still leaves us $85,000,000 short, and already we were in a very difficult position owing to low income. If it is impossible to raise the price of wheat, then I submit we should get some consideration in some other direction. In 1935 the people, applying under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act in Saskatchewan, got their interest rate on mortgages reduced to seven per cent and were given ten years to pay their debts. They have only about four more years to go until these proposals expire. The board that came in in 1936 reduced interest rates to six per cent on land Securities in Saskatchewan, and those people are carrying on on this six per cent basis. Now the present board of review is reducing the interest rate to five per cent and giving the farmers thirteen years to pay, which shows that in its opinion the ability of the farmer to pay his debts is greatly diminished as compared with what it was in 1936. This was decided on before the acreage reduction policy was decided upon.
I have suggested that consideration be given to putting in the Interest Act a provision that the rate of interest on all agreements of sale and mortgages dealt with by the proposals under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act since it has been brought into force in Saskatchewan be reduced to five per cent so that all farmers shall pay on the same basis. It could be done by an amendment to the

The Budget-Mr. Tucker
Interest Act. Since then, however, on further consideration of the situation, especially in the light of the reduced farm income entailed by the wheat policy, I have come to the conclusion that if we cannot take from the farmer of the west his product and market it, a real emergency has been created for him, and on the basis of equality of sacrifice the burden should be passed around. I submit therefore that as a war emergency measure, until we see what will happen next year, at any rate in Saskatchewan, which is hardest hit by the policy, an amendment should be made to the Interest Act, to provide that no interest at all, be charged for 1941 against any agreements of sale or mortgages covering land in that province.
It might be said that lands are not being foreclosed to any great extent in Saskatchewan. But what is happening is this: if by governmental action you deprive the farmers of their income, you may keep them on their farms for a time, but if you allow interest to accumulate against their land and keep on piling up, the time will come when the man and his family will decide that there is no hope for them and there will be foreclosure by consent, or they may move away discouraged. That, surely, is something that should be dealt with by this parliament.
Before the war broke out the situation was recognized as a very serious one, because a predecessor of the present Minister of Finance, the Hon. Mr. Dunning, who is quite familiar with conditions in western Canada, and who probably realized just how bad they were at that time-and they have got worse since then-introduced and helped to get through a bill that would relieve the situation -the Central Mortgage Bank Act. If something should have been done before the war, surely it is more essential than ever that something should be done to-day, because the situation is much worse; and if we are not prepared to deal with the situation by allowing that act to become operative-because it was passed by this parliament but was not brought into existence because of the outbreak of the war-then that is another way in which we have been injured by the war. Therefore, as a matter of emergency, I suggest that for one year, in order to encourage the farmers of western Canada-I should like to see it apply to all western Canada, but at any rate it should be made applicable to Saskatchewan-we should enact a provision that no interest shall accrue during 1941 on agreements and mortgages. That would show the farmers that we are taking a real interest in their problems and that they are not forgotten.
I asked a question with reference to the profits of banks and the answer would show that they can stand it, as a war emergency measure, for one year until we get some sort of plan worked out which would help the farmers. In that regard I would point out that the Central Mortgage Bank Act was referred to a committee of this House of Commons-the banking and commerce committee. Mr. Dunning was there and the matter was thoroughly threshed out and every aspect of it gone into. I am sure that his presence in that committee was very helpful to the ministry of the day and was a means of getting a good bill through the house. The matter could be referred to the banking and commerce committee now to see what should be done as an emergency measure on the question of interest rates so far as western Canada is concerned.
My time is almost up, but there are one or two things I should like to say in conclusion. There is the question of travelling expenses of soldiers. One feature of that, which seems to me to have been overlooked in the past, is that this war is very different from the last one. In the last war the boys enlisted and 'trained in their own province and were then sent overseas. In this war, boys will enlist in Saskatchewan and be sent say to Debert camp in New Brunswick. They are given a furlough of two weeks without any time off for travelling, and that means that they have little over a week at home. I suggest that some consideration be given the question of the distance from home of the soldier who is given furlough. It may be 'the last time he will ever see his loved ones. Surely an extra day or so could be spared to cover travelling time.
Then there is the question of cost of transportation. If the soldier comes from Ontario it costs him very little to get home, but if he comes from British Columbia, Saskatchewan or Alberta, the cost of getting home to see his loved ones on a furlough to which he is entitled is more than a private soldier can afford. I do not say that the soldiers should travel free every time they go on the railway, but on their annual furlough of two weeks transportation should be given them absolutely free so that they can go home; otherwise you are discriminating again against people in the outlying districts of Canada. You cannot get away from that, and something should be done along the line I suggest. I have heard of boys getting furlough in Debert with just enough money to get their ticket home, having to live on a cup of coffee and perhaps a little bit of bread and butter from time to time all the way home. That is not good enough for the people of this
The Budget-Mr. Tucker

country and they will not be satisfied with it. I should like to see something done in this regard.
There is another matter I wish to discuss for a moment, and this may be regarded as the height of temerity; nevertheless I will make a suggestion that goes beyond our borders. During the time that Eire was struggling for her self-government she looked for and got sympathy on this American continent, from the United States and Canada.
To-day, Mr. Speaker, our boys are fighting for the liberty and self-government of Ireland just as much as they are fighting for the liberty and self-government of Canada. Everyone knows that if Great Britain goes down the liberty and self-government of Ireland will be entirely lost; and I submit that if we send our boys overseas to fight not only for our own freedom but for the freedom of Eire, then we in this house have a right to say to the people of that country as a fellow member of the British commonwealth of nations, remembering the sympathy we felt when Ireland was struggling for her self-government: "Now that we are struggling for our liberty, the fact that you will not let us use your bases to help protect our convoys means that some of our boys who are going over there to fight for us and for you are meeting death before they have a chance to strike a blow for freedom." And from my place on the floor of this house I should like to say to the leader of the people of Eire: Remember the days when you fought for freedom. To-day that freedom is more endangered than ever. We are sending our boys to fight for it, and we would like you to cooperate by seeing to it that those boys do not unnecessarily lose their lives while on the way to take part in that struggle.
We realize that Eire must make the decision, but we can send out that call. If the decision is in favour of neutrality, then we can say: Remember how scrupulously Holland maintained her neutrality, but it did not help when Hitler was ready to strike. If Eire says it is wrong to do this thing for various reasons under international law, then we may reply that their great president, Eamon de Valera, was once president of the League of Nations assembly, and in the covenant which Eire signed, as we did, it is provided that each member of the league must help to stop any aggressor. To a certain extent there is an obligation, and there is also an obligation under the Briand-Kellogg pact to cooperate to stop an aggressor. So I should like my humble voice to go from this House of Commons to a fellow member of the British commonwealth of nations, asking that

this matter be considered as carefully and sympathetically as possible under the circumstances.
In conclusion there is just one point with which I should like to deal, and that is the question of the unity of our country.
