speechtext:
I will take only a few
minutes. This is something I feel is important; it is probably the kernel of my speech. Perhaps I should have said it in the beginning, in order to make sure of getting it in.
If we are going to make a real contribution to this effort our unity is probably the most important single factor to be considered. Speaking in Toronto a short time ago Dorothy Thompson outlined Hitler's programme and the plans of the axis. I should like to read a few words from that speech, in which she said that their plans were-
-to set Canadians against the people of the United States; to set labour against capital and capital against labour; the masses against the intelligentsia, and the intelligentsia against the masses; the Irish against the English; the Catholics against the Protestants; the negroes against the whites, the whites against the negroes, and everybody against the Jews, in order that the war which we sought to avoid elsewhere may occur here in an internecine fight, the running amok and berserk of an imprisoned colony.
This is their plan. This always has been their plan, to stir nationality against nationality, race against race, class against class, creed against creed, that their mutual destruction of each other may work out for the glory of Hitler and the grandeur of Japan. . . .
And good men, honest men, unwitting men, work together with the frustrated, the fanatic, the sick, the bitter, the cowardly, the corrupt, the greedy, the selfish, for the end that this civilization may perish from this earth.
I should like to direct particular attention to that statement, that good men, honest men, unwitting men, work with the agents of Hitler to destroy our unity so that we may not put forward our maximum strength in our hour of trial. To-day throughout this country there must be paid agents of Hitler working along these lines, endeavouring to destroy faith in our leaders, in their ability, their honesty, their willingness to do their best in this time of struggle; to destroy faith in one another, to destroy the faith of the people of Englishspeaking origin in those of French-speaking origin, and vice versa; to destroy our faith in democracy, to show that democracy did not solve our problems before the war and that it will not solve them after the war;

The Budget-Mr. Bruce
saying that the boys who are going forward now will come back to ride the rods again; that it is not worth sacrificing anything in this fight; that democracy works only for the people at the top. In this country to-day, as in other countries, there are paid agents of Hitler working along these lines. That was one reason why Hitler found it so easy to carry out some of his conquests. Anyone who reads "Revolution of Nihilism," by Herman Rauschning, will understand how Hitler convinced some of the people of France, for instance, that they had nothing to hope for from democracy as it then existed in that country, that the best thing to do was to let it be destroyed and build again from the bottom. The same thing is happening to-day in Canada. These agents are attempting to destroy our faith in our associates, our faith in Great Britain's ability to stand up to this terrible strain. They are going to the United States and telling the people there that we are not preserving democracy in this country. A resident of Canada, speaking at a labour conference in the United States recently, is reported to have said:
. . . that at present in Canada labour leaders are suddenly taken into custody by the government for no apparent reason, and there are sixty trade unionists in concentration camps along the Ottawa river.
That statement was made by a man who went from this country to speak to labour leaders in the United States, in an apparent attempt to destroy that country's faith in our desire to preserve democracy here. Could anything be more despicable, at a time when we so much need the friendship and help of that nation?
As I have said, undoubtedly there are people, paid by Hitler, who are teaching that doctrine to-day. Then, unfortunately, there are others, honest and unwitting, who are doing more than the paid agents of Hitler, because they speak with authority in their various communities. They are preaching lack of faith in our great leaders and in one another; they are saying that the French-speaking Canadians are disloyal, a statement which I protest against with all the force at my command. That sort of thing is being done by people whom you would expect to be loyal and to give everything they had to our country. They are actually doing the work of Hitler, without knowing it. They are attempting to destroy in the United States the faith which is held in this country; and I should like to add that if the man to whom I have referred is not dealt with adequately I do not think the government will be doing its duty. When we send boys overseas to fight for us at the risk of their lives we must see to it that they are not stabbed in the back at home. It is a pretty serious thing to send our men
overseas; certainly it is important to see to it that our strength at home, our power to uphold them and see to it that they win, shall not be weakened by people going out of the country and making statements of that kind.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank you very much for the extra few minutes you granted me. May I add that if we can only stick together; if we can only preserve our confidence in one another, confidence in those of other racial origins and other religions, confidence in the British people in their heroic struggle, confidence that right will prevail- if we do all that is within our power, united as brothers in a common cause, regardless of racial origin or religious creed, but as Canadians all, then, having dedicated ourselves to the high cause of mankind and the principles we cherish, we can place confidently in the hands of Providence the issue; and right will succeed; wrong will not prevail.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I desire to associate myself with the expressions of sympathy for the British people in the loss of their historic debating chamber of the House of Commons, so ably expressed by the hon. member for Rost'hem (Mr. Tucker), and also for the damage done to that other historic building, Westminster Abbey, containing as it does so many magnificent monuments and the ashes of men who have played so great a part in the history of Great Britain.
I should like also to associate myself with the hon. member in his appeal to the Prime Minister and people of Eire. It seems incredible to some of us of Irish descent that at this time of Great Britain's travail the little island from which some of our forebears sprang should stand out and refuse the mother country the assistance and succour so urgently needed.
I would say just a word of commendation to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) for the able way in which he presented the budget, as well as for the care with which he has distributed the burden of taxation so as to ensure equality of sacrifice. Our citizens will cheerfully shoulder the burden, provided they are convinced that we are making an all-out war effort.
I would ask the Minister of Finance again if he will not now remove the restricting clause, and give the regular tax exemption to the foster parents of British guest children, irrespective of the scheme under which they were brought to Canada. Many of those children are the guests of university professors Who have appealed to me to try to get this relief. Othere are the guests of Canadians who find the increased cost of maintaining them plus the increased income tax a burden
The Budget-Mr. Bruce

they are scarcely able to bear. It is a totally unjust discrimination which should never have been made. I say this with all deference to the Minister of Finance. It is a small concession to make, compared with the announcement over the week-end respecting the modification of the 15 per cent income tax on interest payments to non-residents, so as to exempt payments which are made in United States funds.
May I express the hope also that the minister will give full consideration to the facts presented by the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) and other hon. members regarding the tax on motion picture theatre admissions. I would also plead for the removal of the tax on soldiers' railway tickets, a concession which I think the minister might very well make to offset to a slight extent the persistent refusal to give soldiers free transportation.
May I now divert for a moment to express the satisfaction and pride which all Canadians must feel at the announcement made a few days ago of the selection by Mr. Churchill of one of Canada's most brilliant sons for a position of great importance in the British cabinet. In view of Lord Beaverbrook's rare ability and magnificent achievements in speeding up aircraft production, his promotion was not unexpected. I am sure every hon. member in the house will wish him success in his new post as Minister of State. You know, we claim him as a son of Ontario, because he was born only thirty miles from Toronto.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He lived that down, though.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think perhaps if the truth were known he would be prouder of that than of anything else he has achieved in his lifetime.
We heard yesterday over the BBC that women's contribution to the war effort in Britain is gaining in value daily, that they are now doing eighty per cent of the skilled work in some of the munitions plants. I was glad to hear the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) say over the radio yesterday that plans are being considered for the utilization of women in certain work in Canada's fighting services. There is no doubt that there are many positions which women can fill as well as men. A voluntary women's transport service was organized last summer in Montreal, and in September a detachment was formed in Toronto under the Canadian Red Cross. The Toronto detachment has 160 women members, thoroughly disciplined, who have been driving motor cars, ambulances and other army vehicles, and are able to do all the running repairs to their cars. They are

also trained in first aid and air raid precautions work. For some time Great Britain has had women performing similar services, and they would welcome reinforcements from Canada. Although the members of the Toronto detachment are anxious to go to England to help their sisters there, and for this purpose will pay their own expenses, the Department of External Affairs has refused them passports.
I should like to read the cabled reply from the head of the British motor transport corps to a message sent from the Toronto women's transport service:
Grateful for wire. M.T.C. needs hundreds of drivers, some with pay. Work includes day and night driving, London and provinces. Likelihood foreign service later. Age limit 21 to 43.
I suggest that this voluntary organization be given official recognition by the Department of National Defence, to facilitate their getting overseas for service.
No longer is there any doubt that we need more men, and need them badly and quickly. The Minister of National Defence in his speech over the radio last night gave convincing evidence of this. The minister referred to the changed situation brought about by the fall of Yugoslavia and Greece as the reason why he was now asking for more recruits. Surely, after the fall of France and the epic of Dunkirk, all that has happened since could have been anticipated. If there were any unaware of our danger, the increased shipping losses and the destruction of part of the British House of Commons over the week-end should have convinced them.
Citizens' committees are being set up to secure a definite quota of recruits from each province. The Minister of National Defence is enlisting the members of the house in the first determined drive to get recruits for active service. The minister is confident that the 32,000 men wanted immediately will answer the call to the colours. We hope sincerely that his confidence is not misplaced. But after this drive will come others, and the pressure will have to be increased constantly with steadily diminishing returns. Unfortunately we have been over all this before and certainly should have learned our lesson. In this moment of world crisis it is no longer a case of the individual making up his own mind as to where he can best serve.
From now on it is essential that the manpower of the country be used according to a national service plan. Waste of man-power is the most criminal of all failures in war. It is an unforgiveable waste to have men serving in one place when they are better fitted to serve in another. Surely no one will deny that

The Budget-Mr. Ralston
there should be equality of service and sacrifice so far as that is possible. If we are to enjoy freedom, we must be prepared to fight for it.
I am not a politician and I am speaking only for myself when I call upon the government to take immediate steps to meet the present urgent situation and make available by a national selective process the men necessary to bring our armed forces up to the strength that represents the fighting might of Canada. We should have the compulsory selective service which was visualized by the sweeping powers of the National Resources Mobilization Act passed last June, without the hamstringing clause that prevents men who train under that act from being used wherever the need is urgent. Voluntary recruiting has reached the stage where it is slow, cumbersome and wasteful. I am certain that all parts of Canada will respond to the high patriotic call that the situation now requires. Selective compulsory enlistment is the only fair and efficient way to meet the complex needs of Canada. I venture to suggest, therefore, that this session should not close until we have disposed of this urgent business.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to intervene in this debate, but I understand that my hon. friend has been advocating what he calls national compulsory service. Last night, in an address to the people of Canada, I issued a call for 32,000 men in the next two months. I want to say to my hon. friend that if he could do anything to interfere with that call, possibly to interfere with a full response to it, it would be the advocacy of the measures which he proposes at this time. That is my reason for speaking now. It is something which should not be allowed to go unanswered, to go across this country without a reply.
We went into this war a united people. In October the only province which was called upon to vote with regard to whether Canada should participate, voted overwhelmingly for it. From that time on that province and all other provinces of the dominion have been unitedly behind our war effort. The National Resources Mobilization Act was accepted by this house and by the whole country. The thirty-day plan for compulsory training was accepted by every province including Quebec. The four-months compulsory training plan was accepted by every province. I may say that young men in the province of Quebec have come to the camps in larger surplus numbers perhaps than in any other province. The announcement which I made the other day that men who were in camp for compulsory training would be required to take their places in the coastal defence garrisons or in other duty in Canada has met with a like response.
I cannot understand why at this time, just after I have launched a recruiting campaign, my hon. friend should interject this discordant note into our national unity. I know that he is sincere in his remarks, but I say to him that it is nothing less than a blow at our national unity and, whether he intends it or not, an attempt to undermine it.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I would not think that.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I say that. Why does
my hon. friend now bring this forward? I have asked for 32,000 men. This is the first recruiting campaign that has been put on in Canada in a year and a half of war. This is the first time a call has gone out other than a simple radio address, after which, as my hon. friend will remember, 40,000 men came in within two months. Why does my hon. friend raise this question now and create doubt in the minds of some as to whether or not this is the best way to get men? He used the expression that the recruiting system is cumbersome and expensive.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And wasteful.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What does my hon. friend say with regard to the method of getting money in this country? We had a war loan back in the early days when I happened to be Minister of Finance. Did we pass a law requiring everybody to subscribe, or did we adopt what he calls a cumbersome method, that of going to the people, forming committees and asking them to subscribe their money voluntarily? That was how the first war loan was carried out. The second war loan was carried out in exactly the same way. Another war loan will be on in June. Are we passing a law to require people to give their money, to subscribe so much to that war loan? Not at all; we are asking them to do it voluntarily. We had a war savings certificates campaign and a national war services campaign in connection with which committees were formed all over the country. It might have been cumbersome and it might have been expensive, but that is the way it was done by the free people of Canada.
I do not know why just at this time my hon. friend raises this question. He will see the effect of what he has said. Just at a time when we are asking men to come in voluntarily to enlist he suggests that there is some other and better way whereby some of them may be led to feel that their obligations are not so great. I say to my hon. friend in all seriousness that at this time there is no need of advocating a system such as he suggests. I am advised that there are men in this country and plenty of them to fill all our requirements with regard to the navy, the
The Budget-Mr. Ralston

army, the air force and industrial production. Why at this particular time does he advocate some other system, instead of-I believe he will do this when I ask him-getting out and helping like the rest of us to induce and stimulate the young men of this country to answer the call which the nation has sent out?
If the method which the hon. member has suggested were adopted, it would be a method different from what the commonwealth of Australia has adopted. There is no compulsory national service, to use my hon. friend's words, in Australia for overseas service. In South Africa there is nothing of the kind, and in New Zealand there is nothing of the kind. And in Canada, before the first recruiting campaign is properly launched, does my hon. friend think it the part of wisdom to advocate a system of that kind here? I point out to him that this country in 1917 was seared, was divided, by the very issue which he mentions. We have unity in this country, and I ask my hon. friend to try to help us preserve it, rather than attempting to drive a wedge of disunion into a war effort of which I think Canada ought well to be proud.
I appeal to those who glibly, and perhaps without thought, advocate a change of system at a time when no need for a change has been established, to help in this campaign. I deprecate in public men and in others the attitude of advocating something different for which no need has been established, because I believe it interferes with our war effort, and particularly because it affects the call which has just gone out to the young men of Canada.
And so I appeal to my hon. friend, I appeal to members of this house and to the people of this dominion, to get behind this recruiting effort. I ask them to put it forward in just the same way as they get behind the war loans which are raised, from time to time. I ask them to help make this recruiting campaign a success; not to criticize and suggest some other means when this is the means which has been adopted in a free country- to ask men of free will to come forward and give their services to their country at this time in connection with Canada's war effort.
I do not think I need say more than that at the present time. I do feel that what my hon. friend has suggested is ill-timed and unnecessary.
May I say this to him further? Speaking of the man-power of Canada, we have 3,000,000 more people in Canada to-day than we had when conscription-let us call it by that name [DOT]-was put into effect late in 1917, in the third year of the great war. At the present time I think there are enlisted in the army, navy and air force a number something less than were enlisted in the army, navy and air force

for active service at this time in the last war-and we have three million more people to draw from. Why, then, does my hon. friend attempt at this time to divide the people of Canada and to interject this jarring, discordant note into the campaign which I believe will be supported by the Dominion of Canada? If my hon. friend will put his back into it-and I appeal to him, to my hon. friends all over this chamber, to the people of this dominion-and support this campaign, it will, I am absolutely sure, be crowned with success, just as every other appeal which has been made to the people has been crowned with success in these nineteen months that we have been at war.
Mrs. DORISEW. NIELSEN (North Battle-ford): Mr. Speaker, this is the second budget which has been brought down in this house since we started seriously to enter into the war. It is said that this budget is based upon the ability of our people to pay, but when the whole budget is viewed it cannot help but become apparent to many of us that, rather than being based upon the ability of our people to pay, it is based upon the power of the government to take, which is a very different thing.
We have to-day a government which is very proud of its balanced budget. On the one hand there is a government's balanced budget. But what do we have on the other hand? I would say that the government has found it possible to balance this budget only by making it impossible for thousands of working people to balance theirs. On the one side we have a balanced government budget. On the other side we have unbalanced family budgets, unbalanced homes for many thousands of our working people, unbalanced diets, unbalanced health; and before very long we may find an extra number of unbalanced minds and unbalanced lives because of the pressure of taxation which is put upon our people. What a structure upon which to build a balanced government budget! To me any structure which is built on such a foundation cannot be sound; for nothing can be sound which is built upon the deprivation and unnecessary suffering of our people.
The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker), speaking this afternoon, said that it was not the right of members to criticize this budget, that at such a time as this it would be more correct for all of us simply to fall into line, to agree that the budget was fair, and to let it go by. Yet I feel that at this time it is not the proper thing to fail to point out the inequalities of a budget such as this. The member for Rosthern says that anyone who speaks against the budget or against the government is likely to create disunity.

The Budget-Mrs. Nielsen

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, I distinctly did not say that. There is a distinction between making suggestions that would be helpful and supporting a want of confidence motion.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That was the inference I drew from the hon. member's remarks. This is a budget which creates unequal sacrifice, which is far more than likely to cause disunity among our people. It is very necessary that the government or any body which is financing over a given period should know from what sources their income is to come, and of course the budget is the government's way of determining from what sources its income shall come for the administration of the country's business. But while this government has in this budget the assurance of where its income will come from for government business, what assurance have our ordinary working people of their income through the coming year which is required to maintain their family budgets?
The ordinary working people to-day are faced with a cost of living which, though not rising by leaps, is nevertheless steadily rising. It seems that as every week and every month goes by new demands are made upon our people, new appeals go out to them; and I am afraid that the people will not be satisfied to make the sacrifices which they are being asked to make to-day unless they have not only a guarantee of military victory, which of course they believe is necessary, but the assurance that out of this coming struggle the common working people will go forward to an era of new social security and economic freedom. We have had from our Prime Minister and from other members of the government promises of a new order which shall come forth out of this conflict. But they are promises, Mr. Speaker, and we have had promises in the past, but we have not had fulfilment. In many instances our people to-day are demanding something more definite than the mere promises which are coming out of this conflict. They will sacrifice, but they want to be sure not merely of a vision but of a sound basic structure of a new social economy which will give them greater economic freedom and security than they have ever had in the past. That must emerge; it must come.
I remember reading at one time some speeches made by that old Liberal statesman of England, David Lloyd George. He said on one occasion:
All through history nine-tenths of the people have been grinding corn for the one-tenth, and have been paid with the husks, and have been bidden to thank God that they had the husks.
Through the years of depression the people of Canada have, I believe, become fully
aware that while they, the working people, have produced and have given of their labour and energy in building this country, it is still apparent that they are being paid with the husks and are being bidden to thank God that they have the husks.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does the hon. member
think they would get a better break under Hitler?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not know whether they would or not.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, we do.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The fact remains that if you win a military victory over Hitler but fail to give the people a just recompense for their labour, you will find on your hands what we had as an aftermath of the last war-namely depressions which will give the working people of this country little of the unity, the economic freedom and all that life should give to make it worth living. There is evidence enough to-day that too many of our people are not getting their just recompense. After all, we live in a machine age. Those who work with machines realize that the machine must be given the care and attention which it needs to function properly. It is provided with the best oil or gasoline or whatever it requires for smooth functioning, and when it needs attention it is given repairs so that it can continue to function as it should. To-day many of our working people are treated worse than machines. They do not need gasoline and oil; they need food, clothing and housing; they need those things which will minister to smooth and efficient working and some of the good things which life affords. Machines, especially those used in our war industries, receive the best of treatment; but when you come to examine the conditions of work of many of our people even in the war industries, you find that they are not given the very best of food, housing and clothing which they should have for their smooth functioning and for their working and their living.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let us be specific. Give us some examples.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They depend upon a wage which in these days is inadequate to provide even a minimum of health and strength and security.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What people is the hon. member talking about?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am speaking about working people in industry; I am speaking about all kinds of our working people, in offices and on farms and everywhere where one finds people working in the lower income grades of this country.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Everywhere?
The Budget-Mrs. Nielsen

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Practically everywhere
where they are paid a low rate of wage.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Where? What is the
hon. member referring to?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There are plenty of them in West Calgary.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As regards machines, I
suppose there is more or less a scarcity; we could always do with more of them; but as regards working people, we have too many of them. In the depression we had. To-day we have more working people than, apparently, we can employ. Of course, if some people can manage to get by on a little less money they can get the jobs, while those who have been struggling to obtain higher wages lose their opportunities and their jobs, and can be thrown out, as they were during the depression, on the scrap heap, where, so far as this government cares, they can rot, mentally, morally and physically.
After all, men and women need more than do machines. They need not only food, clothing and shelter; they need food for their minds too. Although many are apt to think that working people do not require these things, nothing the world can afford from its resources of art, of science and of literature, is too good for the working people. Yet what opportunities do they ever have of enjoying these things? Instead, we give them pulp magazines, we give them cheap movies, we give them the funnies, we give them cheap sports. Mussolini was pretty well right when he said, "You must give the working people bread and circuses." We have certainly learned a lesson from Mussolini in the way we treat our working people.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are assisting his cause now.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When any budget is
brought down to this house which demands of our people certain sacrifices, any government which is truly and keenly interested in the people of this country should be certain that there is legislation guaranteeing our people an opportunity to balance their budgets and lead a balanced life. As I have said before, promises are no good; we should have something definite by way of legislation so that our people will have the assurance that out of this conflict will emerge for them a brighter day and a greater freedom.
There are three groups of our working people who are mainly affected. There are our agricultural people, the farmers and agricultural workers; there are our industrial and office workers; and there are our state dependents, those people who are living upon pensions of various kinds. I would say that this

government has failed in what should be an essential thing, if it does not enact certain definite legislation for these groups. I know some hon. members will say, with regard to bringing in social legislation, that we must consider the British North America Act. Why not, since we are a nation, grow up a little more? It is true that we should have veneration for the fine things of the past. We do have. I am sure that all of us have veneration for men like Stephenson, for men like Cartwright with his spinning jenny. But to-day we do not use the spinning jenny; we are in a stream-lined age; yet, when it comes to the constitutionality of legislation we cling to the old and fail to improve and to bring up to date those things which we need in this modern world. It is all very well to venerate the British North America Act. Most Canadians do. They venerate it, however, as something which belongs to the past, but which to-day cannot serve us in our present needs unless it is brought up to date and stream-lined to fit in with a stream-lined world. If we are to have social legislation at the present time, it would appear that, until the British North America Act is changed or revised, we must apply to England for the right to enact such legislation. I say that were we to ask Britain for the right to pass legislation of this kind the application would not be refused. She has said that the nations of the British commonwealth are autonomous. Canada as a nation is growing up and taking its place among the nations of the world, standing on its own feet financially and economically, and surely we should have the right to bring in legislation for our own needs at home. When we applied for the right to enact unemployment insurance it did not take very long to get permission. Why, then, should we not be able to pass legislation which would give more security to our people?
First of all, with regard to our agriculturists and those who depend upon them for their living, it has seemed to me that one thing above all is required to meet in a comprehensive manner the needs of both the east and the west, namely, a natural products marketing act. I am well aware of the fact that legislation of this kind was attempted before and was declared ultra vires, but I say that if to-day we were to apply for the right to enact such a measure, it could not be denied us. With a natural products marketing act, wide and comprehensive enough to take in every sphere of agriculture, we could at least establish a floor below which prices could not drop. We could at least guarantee prices which would be commensurate with the cost of living,

The Budyet-Mrs. Nielsen
and thus give our farmers a little chance to plan ahead and to know how they could best manage to finance their own family budgets, to live decently and to give to their children those advantages to which undoubtedly they have a right.
The second group comprises the industrial and office workers. It seems to me that at this time there is need for a new bill of rights for the working people, particularly in our industries and offices. We should have in this country a minimum wage law. Those hon. members who, like myself, have been receiving letters recently from many of the trade unions will realize the great differences which exist in the various industries. They will realize the terrific fight which our working people are having to put up to obtain for themselves a slight increase in wages which, under present conditions, they so greatly need. Were we to give them the satisfaction of knowing that by legislation we were going to guarantee these things to them, how much more confidence would the working people have.
I know that in the Peck Rolling Mills men are working for just over thirty cents an hour, or roughly $16.58 a week, which few hon. members could possibly agree was a fitting wage on which a man could support a family. To-day it is noticeable in all spheres of industry, even in war industries, that employers, without any shadow of doubt, are definitely flouting certain orders in council that have been passed. One finds to-day that employers are definitely hiring and firing as they will. They are even daring to tell their employees how much, in certain instances, they should contribute out of their salaries for war savings certificates and so on. They are deciding the amount of overtime and the number of hours that employees should work, and in some instances they are even trying to destroy union organization by starting company controlled unions, which is in direct defiance of orders in council passed by the government.
Besides the legislation for a minimum wage there should undoubtedly be an eight-hour day. There should also be legislation to compel employers in these times to carry out immediately the findings of conciliation boards; for that is one way in which to-day one finds employers are doing far less than members of trade unions in trying to bring about settlements in labour disputes.
The third great group of people are the state dependents. There are mothers receiving mothers' allowances, widows of ex-service men, the blind, the ex-service men themselves, veterans, and those on relief. I do not think any member of this house, if he were really honest, could rise in his place in this
chamber and say that any one group of these dependents are receiving enough to enable them to live as people in this country should live. We have our mothers, some of them in Saskatchewan and, I believe, in other places, receiving, roughly, $20 a month, and when one considers the struggle these women have, it seems to me a blot upon us as a people that we can callously disregard these things and let them pass. We have the widows of exservice men. I know that to-day there is a bill-and I am certainly hoping the recommendations which have been made by members of this house will be inserted in it-to give these widows a little better treatment. I have spoken with some of them and I have seen decent, fine women who have gone scrubbing floors in offices in their old age rather than accept relief, because they have been unable to obtain a government pension for themselves.
We have our blind, and there again the pensions are inadequate. How many of our blind people there are who, just because of that one misfortune, are unable to obtain for themselves the education of which they would like to avail themselves if they did not have that disability! Perhaps we have in this country some mute, inglorious Miltons who would give Canada something greater than the country has ever known, if they had the opportunity, the inducement and the help which we as a people should give them.
We have our workers on relief. These people have never had any desire to stay on relief, but to-day they still find themselves in that plight, unable to obtain work or to get into the army, unable to find any employment at all, try as they will. I have seen letters that have come back from the employment bureaux in Saskatchewan saying that their names will be put on the list, and that is all that these people have. Too many of our people have been subjected to these low pensions. Too many have been left to rot on this human junk pile which has been the accumulation of the depression and for which we as a nation are responsible even at a time like this.
There is no doubt about it that instead of legislation of this kind, which I have outlined, to give the people the guarantee which they need if they are to face the future, this budget even cuts down what we might call their husks-and they are still bidden to thank God that they have the husks.
We have the sugar and gas taxes, which possibly affect the poorer people of Canada more than any other tax would do. We have the tax on soldiers travelling on railways. I noticed a cutting in the paper the other day, stating that the combined earnings of the two
The Budget-Mrs. Nielsen

railways for the first quarter of 1941 exceeded the previous comparable record period in 1929 by nearly $500,000. It says that the first quarter's net earnings of the Canadian National Railways were $10,691,565 compared with only $5,437,961 last year; and the first quarter's net earnings of the Canadian Pacific Railway were $8,520,406 this year compared with $5,302,488 last year. Mind you, I am not saying that our soldiers should be given a free pass every time they wish to go from one town to another for a week-end; but, like other members, I feel impelled to say that if we are going to allow our two great railway companies to make profits like these, and deny some of our boys the right to travel home free, perhaps the last time they will travel on Canadian soil, then we are definitely not proving ourselves a government that cares for the common people.
The people are demanding that instead of these taxes upon the lower incomes, we have more of the taxes placed on the higher incomes that can so much more easily bear them. Sometimes it seems to me that the chief concern of this government is to hide from the people that there is corn and that it is well corralled. Possibly in the years to come these matters may be better understood, but already the working people of Canada are beginning to understand that there are ways and means of taxing in this country which would relieve the burden from the lower income groups and give them a little better opportunity.
I noticed a short time ago, in one of the printed lessons and lectures sent out to a cooperative school in one of the provinces- sent out by the department of economics of one of our universities, and I purposely refrain from saying which one, because our professors have to live, too-there was this statement:
Concentration of power and concentration of wealth are more likely to spell doom for us than the tramp of foreign invaders or the oratory of subversive leaders. It is this problem we must face to-day.
Mentally I take off my hat to the professor who in these times had the courage to tell the truth. To-day many Canadian people are asking themselves why we have not one hundred per cent conscription of the wealth of Canada if the crisis is as grave as the government says it is. The government knows perfectly well we do not have that conscription. We have not a one hundred per cent tax on profits. Industry could still maintain itself if that tax were applied; industry can always maintain itself. Have hon. members ever known a time when industry was not able to do so? Certainly not. Industry is able to go on. It is getting war orders; it is getting all the help that can possibly be

given it, but that help is not being given the people working on the land or in the factories. And many people are beginning to wonder to-day, though we are not going to have conscription of wealth, whether before long we may not find ourselves with conscription of man-power. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has denied that. I was very glad to hear that denial, because only recently the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) was asking for conscription, and I noticed that a week or so ago the Toronto Telegram contained an editorial demanding that our boys, who have been conscripted for home defence, should be sent as far as Newfoundland. I was wondering whether perhaps the agitation would not go on; whether, after Newfoundland, the boys who have been conscripted might be sent a little farther away. If some of those who have been conscripted should be sent to the west coast, let us say, and there stop the bullets of the Japanese-bullets made of materials sent from this country and the United States-the people of Canada would feel very badly about it.
Finally, viewing this budget in its entirety, I cannot help saying that I feel it is unjust. This government has not given our common people any guarantee that they will be able to balance their home budgets; yet it has imposed taxes which will seriously affect those in the lower income groups, and at the same time has not brought about any real conscription of wealth.
Perhaps some hon. members may expect me to reply briefly to the blast of hot air which emanated a few days ago from the direction of The Battlefords. I have not taken the matter very seriously. I read the speech, which in turn was read so admirably by the hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Gregory). I read it as I have read various editorials written by the former member for North Battleford, to whom I think the hon. member for The Battlefords must have gone for a little help in preparing his speech. I read that speech with mixed feelings of amusement, pity and contempt. At this time I do not intend to delay the house by reviewing any of the unqualified remarks made by the hon. member; I simply say that time and the people will do that for me.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I and the group with which I am associated wish to see Canada make the most effective contribution humanly possible to this war effort, but with the least amount of sacrifice at home as well as abroad. Nazism is not worthy of having Canadian or empire blood, sweat and tears wasted upon it. We urge

The Budget-Mr. Kuhl
that Canada should exert herself to the maximum to bring this awful holocaust to a successful conclusion in the shortest possible time, but with the least possible amount of sacrifice.
As the greatest arsenal for the empire, under a proper budget Canada could provide at least half as much again, if not double or perhaps even treble, the amount of munitions and supplies that it will be able to contribute under this budget. In peace or war a people can do their best only when they are healthy in body and in mind. People who are undernourished, ill clothed, ill housed; people who are compelled to worry about the welfare of their children and their security both now and in their old age, are in no condition to do what otherwise they would be able to do. Canadians could produce enough foodstuffs, clothing, building materials and so on to keep themselves in the pink of physical and mental condition, and could supply all the war materials needed. This budget, however, will reduce still further the already low standard of living in Canada. People will still be asked to go without in the presence of plenty. Naturally this will increase their health problems and impair their ability to produce.
The hon. member for The Battlefords (Mr. Gregory) has said that the Liberal party is giving the people democratic government because the measures they bring before parliament are brought by a majority party in a parliament elected by the people. That is democracy, of course, but only part of true democracy and a very small part at that. True democracy includes much more than merely the adoption of measures proposed by a majority party in an elected parliament. It all depends upon the definition of the word "democracy." The only definition that I have found thus far that, in my opinion, conveys the true meaning of democracy is this: true democracy is the expression of the policy of the majority. In the light of that definition I say that the Liberal party has not given the Canadian people democratic government, at least since 1935, when it received a mandate from the people of Canada to reform the monetary system. The major appeal to the people by the Liberal party in 1935 was on the question of monetary reform, and a majority of the Canadian people supported the Liberal party in that appeal. Therefore the policy of the majority of the Canadian people was along the lines of monetary reform. Did the Liberal party, as the government, carry out the desires of the majority? Did it give expression to the policy of the majority of the people of Canada? The woefully limited war effort Canada is making is proof positive that the Liberal party has not done so. The woeful inadequacy of government policy to
deal effectively with domestic problems is still further evidence that the desires of the majority have not been carried out.
In my opinion the Liberal party, as soon as they were returned to power in 1935, broke faith with the people who elected them. Like the high priests of pagan idolatry, the Liberal party set about immediately devising new schemes for the deception of the innocent people. The stock of the Bank of Canada was juggled around a bit, and the whole sham was referred to as monetary reform. What a shameful betrayal of the confidence of the people! What base hypocrisy to be practised in the name of democracy! Never was there such great need in Canada as there has been since 1935, and as there was even before that. Never before was there such great need in war as there is to-day. As far back as 1935 the Liberal party received a mandate to order things in such a way that credit and currency would be issued in terms of public need. Nevertheless, to-day currency and credit are not being issued in accordance with the needs of the Canadian people, for either war or domestic purposes. What right, therefore, has the Liberal party or anyone in it to claim that it is giving the people of Canada democratic government?
Whatever is physically possible in Canada can be made financially possible, without a solitary cent of debt. The physical possibilities are not being realized to-day and never will be under the type of budget we are now considering. Therefore I say that the Liberal party is governing Canada contrary to the will of the majority. That certainly is not democracy. It is nothing less than tyranny, and tyranny of the worst type, because it is represented as democracy.
Moreover, in March, 1940, the Liberal party received a further mandate with regard to the war effort. The major issue in the last election was conscription of man-power. That party received a mandate against conscription of man-power. The will of the majority of the people, when they were last consulted, was that there should be no conscription of man-power in Canada's war effort. I wish to remind the Liberals that that is the chie' reason why they are sitting in the house witn their present majority. That majority does not give them the right to contend that the people of Canada approve their financial policy. The supreme issue in the people's minds, when they went to the polls in March, 1940, was conscription of man-power, and that only. The people expressed themselves definitely on that question, and the government has no right to resort to forceful enrolment of man-power until it ascertains the will of the majority, either through a plebiscite or through some other similar means.
The Budget-Mr. Kuhl

While I am on that subject, I'wish also to.remind the Conservative party in the house of that fact. Conservatives are constantly rising in their places and urging the government to conscript the man-power of the nation. Do they not intend to respect the mandate of the people, either? If they do, then why are they constantly urging the government to conscript the man-power of Canada, when they know full well that only a year ago the majority of Canadians voted definitely against this policy. The Conservative attitude indicates to me that they are just as contemptuous of the will of the majority as are the Liberals.
The government has no mandate for the conscription of man-power, yet it is resorting to the most inequitable and the vilest form of conscription that could be used, namely, economic pressure. Through a discontinuance of the dominion's quota of relief payments, through unnecessarily increased tax burdens, through the increased cost of living, the only alternative to enlistment left for a large number of our men is to beg, steal or starve. This is the most unjust and the vilest form of conscription that could be used. It discriminates against the most unfortunate class in society, those who through no fault of their own have no economic security whatever, or are trying to live on subsistence incomes.
If the government wishes to have conscription, then I say, let it use an honest, fair and above-board policy. Even then, as I have already indicated, I say it has no authority and no right to use a just conscription policy until it receives a further mandate from the people on that issue.
Many hon. members have showered the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) with verbal bouquets upon the presentation of his budget. When one considers what the minister has accomplished within the narrow confines of an obsolete, out-moded and out-of-date financial policy, one cannot help giving him all the credit which is due to him. But the point which the social credit group in the house has been making constantly is that if the minister had not permitted himself to be hemmed in by such a woefully inadequate financial policy, he would be much better off, and the people of Canada would be able to do much better in their war effort, as well as in the solving of their domestic problems.
The government is constantly appealing to our people to put forth a greater effort. The people are over anxious to do more. The files of every hon. member contain dozens of letters from people who are just begging for
tMr. Kuhl.]
an opportunity to use their hands and their heads or both. The financial policy of the government prevents their doing so. The people are ready and willing to do the work, but there is simply no opportunity for them, unless the government issues sufficient money. No budget proposals thus far have done this, and neither will the proposals in the budget now under debate. Not only is it a crying shame, but it is a crime for the government to refuse to adopt policies which would enable thousands of people in Canada to make the contribution they are so anxious to make. I am willing to give the government all the credit due it for that measure of organization of Canada's resources and man-power it has already effected. But as I have already stated, if the government had had a proper financial policy, the results thus far would have been at least doubled, and possibly trebled, with very little additional effort on the part of the ministry.
If the Minister of Finance develops a headache in the preparation of a budget of this type, then I say it is no one's fault but his own. I am quite satisfied that as a result of policies included in this budget many of the common people will develop more than a headache in trying to make their payments. So far as the minister personally is concerned, I am sure his task would be infinitely lighter and much more pleasant if he took his orders from the people who elected his government rather than from St. James street and Wall street.
Many hon. members on the government side of the house have expressed resentment at the criticism of the government's policy by hon. members of the opposition. I wish to repeat what I have said on previous occasions, that if the government wishes to be immune from criticism it must introduce measures which will remove rather than accentuate existing injustices. If every man-hour of work and every pound of material available and necessary to the war effort were being utilized, I am quite sure there would be little if any criticism from the opposition. Furthermore, if every man-hour of work and every pound of material that cannot be used or are not necessary for the war effort were used to improve domestic conditions in Canada, I believe there would be still less criticism from opposition members. But neither the general policies of the government nor its present budgetary proposals will permit the attainment of either of these objectives. And I say that just so long as that position obtains, I shall consider it my duty as a member of the house to protest against these unnecessarily unsatisfactory conditions.

The Budget-Mr. Kuhl
Because the budget does not permit a maximum war effort, and because its proposals will force the people of Canada still farther into the clutches of their domestic enemy, the money powers, I consider this budget unpatriotic. Not only is it unpatriotic, but it is unreal. It is nothing but a cold, callous arrangement of figures with little relationship to human life in Canada. It is merely a statement of what the government proposes to do with the pen-and-ink dollars which the banking monopoly choose to put into circulation in Canada.
There is no attempt whatever to establish a relationship between the financial proposals of the budget and the ability of the Canadian people to produce materials, either for the war effort or for the solving of their domestic problems. The minister states that if the war expenditures for the fiscal year 1941-42 reach the original estimate, they will be in the neighbourhood of two billion dollars. What does that statement mean in the real sense? Does it mean that two billion dollars worth of goods is the extent of the war supplies which the Canadian people will be able to produce during the coming year? If it does mean that, then I am quite satisfied with the amount of two billion dollars.
But I do not believe it means that, because there are thousands of available man-hours of work still being wasted, and that will be the situation next year at this time. Just so long as there are people without work or only partly employed, the budget proposals will not be providing for a maximum war effort. Why should the estimated expenditure for the coming year not be two and a half billion dollars, or three billion dollars, or even four billion dollars? The minister has not produced any facts to indicate that two billion dollars worth of materials will be the limit of Canada's ability to produce war materials during the coming year. So long as materials can be produced, why should there be any limit to the amount of money that Canada will use? So long as we have men and materials, it is just as ridiculous to say that we have no more dollars as it is to say that we cannot build a road because we have run out of yardsticks, or that we cannot use any more lumber because we have run out of feet. If the minister had stated that our war effort was being limited to two billion dollars because that will finance all the ships, all the aeroplanes, all the tanks, all the guns, all the munitions, and all the clothing that the people of Canada are physically capable of producing for war purposes, then his statement would have meant something. As it is, I do not believe that there is any real significance to the minister's budgetary statement.
The expenditure for non-war activities is to be limited to less than half a billion dollars. The same reasoning applies here. If half a billion dollars represents all the services which the government is physically able to supply to the people after war requirements have been met, then I can understand the minister's proposal. But again I contend that he has not produced any facts to indicate that half a billion dollars worth of services are all that the government can supply to the people. I should like to refer to the minister's budget address, as reported on page 2343 of Hansard. Referring to the deficit which was anticipated for the coming year, he said:
For our present purposes, I think, we will not be far wrong if we assume the figure to be $1,500,000,000. It is unnecessary for me to emphasize the staggering task which this places upon the Canadian people. It can be done without any doubt, but it will not be easy.
Then a little further down on the same page he made this statement:
I need not tell the house that to raise such an amount will require such a great increase in the savings of the Canadian people that the help of every man, woman and child will be required.
I object to the inference in those statements. They are not only incorrect; they are extremely misleading. If the minister had said that in order to meet the added requirements for war purposes, all the people of Canada must work nine or ten hours a day instead of eight, that the school children must go to work because there are not sufficient workers, then I could understand him. As I have said before, the people of Canada are more than anxious to work; they are crying out for opportunities to work; they are anxious to apply their hands and their heads, and they are prepared to work long hours if necessary. It is the duty of the government to provide money or to see that it is provided in order that the people may have an opportunity to apply themselves. Unless the financial policy of the government is such that sufficient money is put into circulation, all the people of Canada cannot put forth the effort they would like to, no matter how anxious they may be to do so.
The minister has stated that the raising of the money will be a staggering task. That is untrue. The raising of money is the simplest task in the world because that is the cheapest commodity which man has ever used. To-day money consists of nothing but coloured water and cheap paper. Money is practically costless to produce. The banks raise all the money they need at a cost of merely the ink, paper and clerical work involved. At no cost to themselves the banks have bought approximately one-half billion dollars worth
The Budget-Mr. Kuhl

of interest-bearing government war bonds. The money which they used to purchase these bonds was manufactured out of coloured water and cheap paper, just the same as another manufacturer would manufacture shoes. I wish to remind the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) as well as the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene) that the governor of the Bank of Canada said this himself When testifying before the committee on banking and commerce in June, 1935, he made this reply to the following question:
When a million dollars worth of bonds is presented to the bank a million dollars of new money or the equivalent is created?
Mr. Towers: Yes.
The other day my colleague, the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Jaques) emphasized the point that this creation of fountain-pen money is not a theory, that it is the fact that over ninety-five per cent of the money which Canada and all other countries use is nothing but pen-and-ink money. If the government would take back the sovereign prerogative of creating the money of the nation and exercise it itself, then it could raise money at the cost of merely the paper, ink and clerical work. Again I say that the raising of money by the government would be the simplest task in the world.
The Minister of Finance implied in the statement which he made on page 2343 of Hansard that this deficit of $1,500,000,000 would have to be raised from the savings of the people of Canada. As my colleague the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) has already pointed out, this will not be the situation. The common people of Canada simply will not have the funds after they have paid their taxes and taken care of their own requirements. The money will not be in existence, and it will be obtained in the same fashion as the $500,000,000 was obtained from the chartered banks. The banks will manufacture the money and buy the government bonds with their own manufactured pen-and-ink money.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This one and a half billion dollars required by the minister will be raised in identically the same fashion as the $500,000,000 was obtained. The chartered banks will create the money, and the debt will be charged to the common people, who in turn will be asked to pay a perpetual toll to the banking monopoly for the use of the people's own credit. I consider such a policy an abomination. The creation of money is the crown's prerogative, and all money ought to be created by the government's own institution, the Bank of Canada. The present financial policy of the government asks the people to pay several times over, financially, for a debt which they have paid fully, physically, and I cannot conceive of a greater injustice that could be done to a people than to be forced, they and their children, to continue to pay a toll to a private money monopoly for a war for which they have already paid fully in blood, sweat and tears. I see absolutely no reason for a national debt in peace time or for a war debt in war time.
I was tremendously inspired by the address of the Prime Minister of Australia when he spoke in this house, but he made one statement which caused me to reflect. His statement or the implication of it was that we ought to carry through this struggle even if the result were bankruptcy for us. I quite agree that we must press forward in this struggle and continue the war effort at all costs. But I do not believe that bankruptcy should necessarily follow. When this war is over, regardless of how long it lasts, our resources will be in a better position to be used for the benefit of the people of Canada than they were before the war started. Our agricultural soil will be in just as good a condition as it was in before, and if all the rest of our resources are properly managed during the war, we should have a far greater capacity to produce the necessities of life after the war is over than we had when it started. No nation is bankrupt until either the people have all perished or unless it is without resources. If all our minerals have been consumed, if all our forest wealth has been used up, if all the resources of the country have been consumed, then the nation is bankrupt. But certainly that will not be the situation with Canada or with any other part of the empire after this war is won, and I see no reason why there should be any suggestion that in order to win this war we must go bankrupt. The financial balance sheet may be arranged in such a way that it will indicate that we are financially bankrupt. But that is not true in a real

The Budget-Mr. Bence
sense. That will be the situation only because we have been using during the war a financial policy which does not reflect the facts. If the financial policy were such that it reflected the facts, it would indicate that when we have paid for the war in blood, sweat and tears, there is nothing owing and the accounts would be marked "Canada's part in the war paid for in full."
If the government had carried out the mandate which it received from the people in 1935, and had used the Bank of Canada since that time and were using it to-day, in the fashion in which the people of Canada were led to believe it was going to be used, then this war to-day could be financed without debt, and not only that but the war effort could be at least doubled or trebled. It would also have enabled the government to deal effectively with all the agricultural problems not only of the west but of the whole country. The problem is merely one of finance, and not one of dealing with physical things. There is no reason why, if the government controlled the financial policy of this country and used the Bank of Canada properly, instead of bonusing the non-production of wheat, it could not have bought every bushel of wheat which the farmers were able to produce, paid them the cost of production plus a fair profit, and stored that wheat in properly constructed elevators until such time as it could be disposed of. Whatever is physically possible can be made financially possible. There is no lack of man-power thus far; there is no lack of gravel or cement. Then why could not elevators have been constructed, using our idle resources and our idle man-power, and the grain stored in these elevators? The time will probably come when we shall be sorry that we ever thought of restricting production in this country. The storage of other kinds of food could have been handled in the same fashion.
A proper Bank of Canada policy would have enabled the government to provide the highest possible standard of living for the people during the war. Naturally there must be sacrifices, but what many of the people of Canada are being called upon to endure to-day, as has been emphasized and re-emphasized in this house, is unnecessary sacrifices. So long as there is the wherewithal to satisfy the desires of the people of this country, there should be no lack of funds to enable them to satisfy their desires. If the Bank of Canada were used as it should be, the government could to-day be providing our soldiers with free transportation at least for their annual furlough. Furthermore, the government would be enabled to set up policies to deal effectively with post-war problems. But as it is 14873-173
now, there is no policy to deal with post-war problems. The Bank of Canada, if properly used, would have enabled the government to finance any undertaking without debt.
In conclusion, the British empire is to-day facing the greatest crisis of its history. The help of every man, woman, and child in Canada is necessary to avert the danger. The Canadian people are ready, willing, and almost overanxious to exert themselves to the maximum, but they cannot do so until the government adopts a proper financial policy. The government has not done so. Until it does so, I consider it my duty to oppose and protest against the existing financial policy.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At
the outset of my remarks I should like to add my words of endorsement to those already uttered in this house with respect to the principle of this budget, as being necessary and in keeping with the sacrifices which are required at this time. It may well be that, when another year has rolled around, even this budget, involving what seems to us a colossal sum, will by comparison have merged into insignificance with respect to what is needed then. Who knows? We know this, however that no financial sacrifice is too great to make in order to save our bodies, our souls and our empire from conquest.
In the early stages of the war, the government determined upon a pay-as-we-go policy, and since that time it has endeavoured, so as far as it has been able, to adhere to that policy. I agree with the soundness of many of the arguments which are put up in favour of it, but I suggest that we can carry it too far with respect to the future economic wellbeing of the people. The type of taxation we have in effect at the present time is confiscatory. It is levied; it is taken; and it is gone for good. And there are so many taxes that it keeps us busy trying *o keep track of them. In the first place wc have our city and municipal taxes, with their levies on real estate, business, water, light, amusements and many other things, including poll tax. Then we come to the provincial taxes with their claims on income and on real estate: gas tax, sales tax, corporation taxes, public revenue tax, and many others. Next there is the wider field of dominion taxation, with its direct and indirect imposts and their multitude of claims. To mention just a few, there are income tax, national defence tax, excise tax, sugar tax, and now we have the succession duty tax, and a host of others about which the average man in the street knows nothing beyond the fact that he has to pay them.

The Budget-Mr. Bence

But all these taxes are only a start, so far as the claims on a man's pocket-book are concerned. Continually, worthy war and charitable appeals are being made, and the people of this country are being asked to dig more and more deeply into their pockets all the time. Any one tax or any one appeal may not in itself appear too great; but when we come to the total of these appeals and these taxes, we find that the average man has little or nothing left to put aside for his old age or provide necessary and vital protection by way of life insurance for his family. It is for this reason that, I suggest, the government may carry this principle too far.
We must realize that there are in Canada to-day many men and women who are at their pea'" so far as earning capacity is concerned wit* respect to age, mental and physical qualifications, and the opportunity which is given to their particular generation. The government should consider permitting these men and women to save at least part of the fruits of their labours so that they may have something to live upon when that peak is past, when they are older, when their mental and physical powers are not so great, and when the opportunities which are now present will not be available to them. It is important that w'e should endeavour to eliminate the sense of frustration which many of these people must have. Not a few of them have been without gainful employment for many years. They now find themselves in the position of returning to a fruitful occupation, of being able to earn a livelihood. They look forward to a few' years of activity, which may end when the war is over or even before that time. They realize at the same time that the taxation which is being imposed will not allow them to put something aside for their old age, will not allow them to feel that they can exist at that time without having to depend upon charity.
This does not mean-and I am by no means suggesting it-that we do not require every cent which we can raise at this time. We do require it. But what I am suggesting is that, at least so far as this increase in taxes is concerned, and particularly with respect to some of the lower income brackets-although I do not propose that it necessarily be confined to them-the amount which people are now earning over and above what they require to live upon should not be entirely confiscated by way of taxation, but that, at least in part, it should only be borrowed. The fact that I believe in this principle is one of the reasons why I so enthusiastically endorsed the war savings campaign. I did everything I could personally to support it, and I urged upon the people with whom I discussed it the

advisability and urgency of putting their money into it. I felt that the more money they put into the war effort by way of war savings certificates, the less they would be called upon to put in by way of taxation; and that seemed to me to be a sound principle, particularly because the war savings scheme was aimed to give people of small incomes an opportunity of making their contribution.
Savings attain several useful purposes, particularly at the present time. In the first place, of course, they help us to buy necessary war materials; second, they give those who save a nest-egg which will help them after the war is over, and also enable them to keep the wheels of industry turning and thus to alleviate the post-war depression which seems inevitably to follow every great conflict. Third-and I think this is the most important -they give more people in Canada a material stake in this dominion, and a material stake will be a great incentive, after the war is over, for the people who have it to assist us in keeping our country on a sane economic basis in the transition from a war to a peacetime economy.
Consequently, I suggest that this government, in the present budget, and in any successive budgets in which the taxation is considerably in excess of normal, should make arrangements to pay back at least part of that excess as soon as the war is over, and that it should adopt the policy which has been referred to in this chamber, which has been so long advocated by John Maynard Keynes, the English economist, and which was recently adopted by the English people. Sir Kingsley Wood, in his budget speech in the British House of Commons a short time ago, referring to the matter of the reduction in what they call the personal allowance and the earned income allowance, made this statement:
I am proposing therefore that the extra tax which any individual will pay by reason of the reduction in the personal allowance or earned income allowance will be offset after the war by a credit which will then be given in his favour in the post office savings bank.
The proposal in the British budget is that the increase in taxation will be paid back to the taxpayer after the war, without interest.
Some may point out that the comparison between income tax levied in Great Britain and that levied in Canada shows that the British people are paying considerably more in proportion by way of taxes than we are. I believe this point was referred to the other day by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews). But a comparison of income taxes does not give us a fair picture of the comparative amounts paid by the two peoples because, as I understand it, our taxation is

The Budget-Mr. Bence
spread over many more fields, and we pay more in proportion in certain other fields than they do. It is true they concentrate on income tax. We have not as high an income tax, but we do derive funds from many other fields, a great many of them by way of indirect taxation.
