speechtext:
This question was referred to by the Ottawa Journal in an editorial the other day, and that newspaper made a pertinent observation which I should like to read. Referring to the difference in income tax between the two countries, it said:
But these figures, indicating a more heavily taxed Britain, must be qualified by certain facts. To begin with, the taxpayer in England pays but one income tax. In Canada-up to the present, at any rate-the taxpayer pays additional income tax to the province. Then, in Canada there is a sales tax of 8 per cent, whereas Britain has no sales tax. Also in Canada there are heavier customs taxes, plus an import tax of 10 per cent, over and above all customs taxes. Finally, Canadian property taxes-real estate-are on the whole higher than in Britain.
Taken all in all, therefore, the average Canadian's taxes are probably not far below those of the average Englishman.
Let no one make any mistake about this. We are paying very heavy taxes to-day under this budget, and I suggest that it puts us in a rather difficult position, when taxation is imposed in the indirect way in which it is in this country, because unscrupulous people can take advantage of the fact that we have spread our taxation over so many fields, to use things like the income tax, as between Canada and Great Britain, to make invidious comparisons to our disadvantage with respect to things like the income tax. Consequently, it seems to me-and I make this suggestion to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley)-that we should endeavour, so far as we are able, to bring home more clearly to the people of this country and to the peoples of other countries exactly how much of our income is going towards war materials and matters connected with our effort in this great struggle.
I do not intend to enter at this time into any analysis of the various arguments put forward by Mr. Keynes in favour of his proposal. It is sufficient to state that it met with the endorsement of the British House of Commons. There they felt that the most important thing achieved by this policy-and it is none of the three I have mentioned so far-was that it assisted materially in restraining the practically ungovernable tendency towards inflation which seems to exist in war
14873-173}
time. The people who are charged with such matters, such as the Minister of Finance, have as their task in war time, in endeavouring to keep down inflation, the question of reducing the ability of the public to spend that extra amount of money which is put into circulation as a result of increased war activity. Taxation is one of the means whereby they reduce the ability of the public to spend, but a far better way would be, of, at least to a certain extent, borrowing that money from the great mass of the people who are paying in the smaller income-tax brackets and not confiscating it all.
Sir Kingsley Wood, in his budget speech, said with respect to his proposal to pay back this extra amount of taxation:
The primary object of these proposals is not to obtain taxation for taxation's sake, nor to raise revenue for the sake of the revenue, but to make a considerable cut in purchasing power during the war, and thus to avoid the ever present dangers of inflation, which would affect most of all those with the lower incomes.
We have to-day hidden taxes on too many of our essentials, taxes that hit everyone just as hard as if they had been put on in the form of income tax, and even harder, and I repeat the suggestion that the government seriously consider the question of levying taxation in such a way that we would see more clearly how much of our income is going to the state. Let us have more direct and less indirect taxation, and let us pay back part of it after the war is over, so that the wealth of the nation at that time will be in the hands of many and not concentrated in those of a few.
So far as I am personally concerned, speaking as one of the comparatively younge! generation, it might appear foolish for me or members of my generation to suggest that we should postpone any part of the cost of this war. Speaking as a Canadian and speaking generally, however, I think I can safely say that the future generations of this country are going to owe something to those who are making the sacrifice to-day in order that those future generations may live in a free world.
I do not propose to enter into any discussion of specific matters in the budget. Like other hon. members, I shall reserve until we are in committee any comments I have to make on a number of such subjects. There are certain inequities arising in connection with the raising of national revenue which seem to me to be quite apparent, and I cannot understand why they have not already been ironed out, but as I say, I shall take the privilege of making some remarks about them when we are in committee.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
The Budget-Mr. Bence

After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose at six o'clock, I had finished dealing briefly with the suggestion that the government should relax its pay-as-you-go policy, at least to the extent that the amount which a man earns over and above what is required to live on, should not be entirely confiscated by way of taxation but, in part, should be only borrowed so that he might have something on which to live after the war is over.
I wish now to take advantage of the fact that this is one of the few occasions on which hon. members are privileged to discuss general matters, to present a suggestion in connection with the general economic set-up of the *country, with particular reference to the way in which I think the wheat problem might be eventually solved. During the last number of weeks we have heard presented in this house various policies that have been suggested with regard to a solution of the wheat problem. These have included the policy of the federation of agriculture, the policy of the wheat pools, the plan of the western prairie provinces; and of course we considered at some length the proposal-the most inadequate proposal, I submit-of this government. No matter from what angle we considered any of these proposals, whether we took the one we liked best or the one we preferred the least, we were necessarily led to the conclusion that any one was but a temporary expedient, just a medium for postponing for a year or two the final day of reckoning. I am, therefore, convinced that we should take definite steps now which will eventually result in diverting a large part of the western labour supply into channels other than agriculture.
It is trite to say that in order to exist we must produce something that can be exchanged for some other sort of wealth. We know that at the present time we are producing something which, to a large extent, cannot be exchanged for another type of wealth. In addition, it is quite apparent that with the state of self-sufficiency which was attained with respect to foodstuffs by the countries of Europe after the last war, we shall not, after this war, with the possible exception of a short period, be able to sell as much wheat or other foodstuffs to Europe as we have in the past. Because of this fact, and because of the further fact that we have greatly improved our methods of production in western Canada, we do not require the labour that we formerly did to produce our wheat crop. Yet we have done very little indeed, from an economic point of view, to endeavour to divert that

excess of labour in western Canada into channels entirely separate and apart from agriculture.
During the committee stage of the war appropriation bill, there was a great deal of discussion by hon. members as to the advisability and, in fact, the necessity of greater war production in various parts of the country. With those sentiments I was in hearty accord, because I believed that if any part of Canada were idle and it could produce essentials for war or any other purposes, we should put that part of the country to work. The necessity for the diversification of industry, by spreading war projects all over the dominion, has received a considerable amount of attention from many sections. I did not take part in the discussion on this subject when the war appropriation bill was under consideration, because when I first had au opportunity of speaking in this house, last November, I urged upon the government the advisability of turning a large part of the vast labour supply of western Canada from agriculture into essential war industries, and at that time I pointed out that to bonus non-production, idleness and useless overproduction, is economically unsound. At a time when we require an all-out war effort it is senseless to allow these men, many of them artisans and mechanics, to fritter away their time in producing something that cannot all be used.
It would appear from the discussions that have taken place in this house that many sections of Canada are not fully occupied. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that when an allout war effort is required, it should be the function of the government to put those idle parts of the dominion to work. But there does not appear to be anyone who is making it his sole job to examine this problem from the dual point of view of war production and the country's internal economic welfare. I do not suggest for one moment that the blame can be placed upon the shoulders of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe), because he has his hands full in meeting war requirements'-without worrying about any dual purpose. Consequently I suggest to the government that this might be made a matter of general governmental policy, and that a portfolio-for the sake of a better name let us call it the portfolio of economic welfare- be created and placed in charge of a man whose sole job would be to study the economic set-up of Canada with a view to utilizing all the energy and all the materials of the country by diverting them from non-essential into essential production, of course having regard to the opportunity that is given us to-day because of war production

The Budget-Mr. Jaques
requirements. His job, for example, would be to examine the wheat problem in relation to the general economic set-up and to determine the best way of diverting or directing the energy and the brains that are available in western Canada, and that are not now being used, into essential fields of productivity.
The same thing would hold true for other sections of Canada. We heard a fairly lengthy discussion here by various maritime members with regard to the advisability and urgency of increasing shipbuilding in the maritimes. One of the strong arguments put up-and I thought it was a sound one-was that in addition to producing ships for war purposes, it would give employment and bring the maritimes back to some of the economic glory they enjoyed in the past. We in western Canada have great possibilities for producing war supplies, and for industrial work. We have potential power through our gas, coal and rivers. We have space; we have safety; we have brains; and, above all else, we have man-power willing and eager to apply itself. We have young farmers who, because of their mechanical background, are ideally suited to work in factories. I suggest that even if, because of freight rates it costs a little more to produce such commodities in western Canada, it is better to bonus for the production of essentials than for the production of non-essentials, as we are doing at the present time.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) upon the able manner in which he presented the budget, but I cannot agree with much of the matter contained in his proposals.
I do not intend to deal with the details of the budget, I have left that to others. I should like, however, to deal with the matter which is the subject of our amendment, namely, the failure of the government to use the Bank of Canada to help finance the war. I had thought the House of Commons had a fair understanding of our ideas in that respect. I believe we have been hammering on them for the last five or six years. Therefore, when I attended a meeting addressed by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Thorson) in Manitoba recently, I was surprised when he said that the social crediters in the House of Commons had been talking for five years, and that nobody was any wiser as a result of what they had said.
That reminds me of a social credit meeting I once attended. At the conclusion of the speaker's remarks, the chairman announced that the speaker would be glad to answer any questions. A man in the audience rose in his
[Mr. Bence.?
place and said that he had greatly enjoyed what had been said, but asked if the speaker would explain again how money was created. So the speaker went through his explanation again. However, at the conclusion of that explanation the man again said, "I am sorry, but I still don't understand it." So the speaker explained it again, and still the man did not understand. The chairman then intervened and said, "I shall explain it for you," and proceeded to do so. But the man again replied, "I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, but I still fail to understand." That was too much for the chairman, so he stepped off the platform, went up to the man and said, "I'll tell you why you don't understand it; it is because you are just a plain ruddy fool!"
There are none so deaf as those who will not listen. I am sure, however, that that does not apply to a large number of hon. members; and of course I am quite sure it does not apply to the minister.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member ought to eliminate everybody.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That reminds me of another meeting I attended in one of the larger towns in Alberta. That was a meeting of the so-called People's League, which was formed at that time to oppose the social credit movement in Alberta. On the platform were the Conservative leader in the province, a former federal Liberal member from Calgary, and a former socialist member from Alberta who sat in this house. There they were, all on the platform together, united in their opinions as to the danger social credit held for Alberta. The socialist put it this way-

He put his arms round the
Conservative leader's shoulders and said, "We may have had differences of opinion in the past, but when we consider the danger to our province and the danger to our women and children from the government at Edmonton, our differences fade into insignificance."
That was the year Mr. Chamberlain went to Munich. There were at that time a million Canadians on relief. We were at that time within a year of war with the greatest military power the world has ever known. There was not at that time in Canada a single tank; not one plane was being made. I heard a
The Budget-Mr. Jaques

former Minister of National Defence say in the house that the Canadian flying corps had ceased to fly.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They were just fluttering.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Not a gun was being made in Canada at that time. Yet we were within one year of the war. The danger seen by those misguided people on the platform was nothing but a threat to a financial system which, unknown to them, but plain to everybody who understood it, had already placed Canada and the empire on the very verge of destruction.
There is no question that for years democracies, as to their policies and their way of life, have been controlled by the financial interests. There is proof of that. But that control is only another variation of the control formerly held by those who controlled religion. In the middle ages men held the world in control by fear of eternal fire and damnation. At one man's word a nation was ready to fall on its back; it was excommunicated. The power which those few men held was theirs because of the ignorance of the masses of the people. When, through the printed word, knowledge was spread, the people began to doubt these ideas, and in order to maintain their control these tyrants said, "Well, if the fear of fire in the next world is not sufficient, we will see what a little fire in this world will do," and so they proceeded to burn and torture those who ventured to differ from them. But there was the natural reaction. This did not stop the people from criticizing. They said, "If we are going to be burned in this world as well as in the next, such a system is not worth a candle, let alone a bonfire." So it was only a matter of time before that control passed away. That control, however, was then taken over by the controllers of finance, and it has been growing stronger and stronger from that day to this. As knowledge has spread, people have risen here and there, books have been written, people have spoken in parliaments and at public meetings, and gradually more and more are becoming enlightened as to the control exercised by finance.
I should like to quote from the parliamentary debates of the commonwealth of Australia, the first session of 1940. I remember that a member of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation group held out to us that the New Zealand government had solved the financial problem and that there was no need for the proposals of social credit. I should like to quote from a statement by a senator in the Australian senate. He was speaking on the same idea as this amendment; that is, he was advocating that the national bank of
[Mr. Jaques.l	.
Australia should help finance the war by the issuing of interest-free credit. Another senator, Senator Hays, asked him:
Why does not the government of New Zealand issue an interest-free loan?
Senator Darcey replied:
For the simple reason, as I explained to the honourable senator, that the government "sold out" to the banks.
He then went on to explain:
When Mr. Nash -went to London, he found that he could not convert any of the loans that had been raised by New Zealand, because his government had made a radical change in the dominion's financial policy. In those circumstances, Mr. Nash had to take what he could get.
The leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Coldwell) made a statement which I should like to correct. I am not saying that he made it deliberately, but there is no doubt that he was misinformed. He said:
According to social credit expert Byrne society is like a pyramid. The people on the outside are the circumference, and at the top there must be one directing mind. That one mind must give orders and all must take instructions right down to the outer fringe.
What Mr. Byrne did say is contained in a pamphlet entitled "Alternative to Disaster". I quote:
The two forms of organization applicable to society are the pryamidal, involving centralization of control, and the democratic, under which the wishes of the majority prevail. The pyramidal type is so termed because it can be pictured as a grouping of people in the form of a pyramid at the apex of which is a supreme authority dominating the entire structure through lesser executives working under him. Democratic organization can be pictured as a grouping of people in the form of a circle, in which administration at the centre is dominated by the majority at the circumference. This necessarily involves the ability of the majority to accept or reject administrators according to the satisfaction or otherwise they experience from their administration.
I desired to make that correction. I think the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) has explained quite well the reason for our amendment, 'but there is one point which I should like to make. I wish to refer to the large numbers of war bonds which have been purchased by the banks merely through the process of writing cheques on themselves. Just as that money has been created by a stroke of the pen when they acquired the bonds, so will that money be destroyed when the banks sell the bonds to the people at the end of the war. These bonds owned by the banks will be a dangerous weapon of deflation after the war. We have always had deflation

The Budget-Mr. Jagues
after a war, and in the past this has been blamed upon the damage caused by the war as well as other things.
The real reason is that war creates an enormous debt. War also causes inflation, and those who own the debt see to it that, after the war, money is deflated so that the debts are inflated. That is the object of post-war deflation, and this is always done at the cost of the misery and suffering of the masses of the people. When a Liberal member from Alberta was speaking in this house the other day he seemed to regard an amendment such as ours as being unpatriotic. He asked the Speaker what he thought of our soldiers being paid in money which he referred to as "trash". That is to say, money bearing the stamp of the king and issued by this sovereign parliament was trash, while money created by a private bank was sound money. I should like to quote what Prime Minister Menzies said when he was asked about the war financing in Australia. He said:
We are raising what we consider the maximum amount by taxation and taxation is very liigh now. Then we raise money from *the savings of the community through loans. We supplement the two sources by using the central bank credit, subject to the checks imposed on the inflationary effect by use of the taxing powers and by a system of price regulations which we had in operation since three days after the war broke out.
I have heard members say, and quite rightly, that they were greatly inspired by the address of Mr. Menzies. According to this statement of Mr. Menzies-and I assume that he was correctly reported-in Australia the government are using the credit of the national bank of Australia. That is all that we propose to do here, and there is nothing revolutionary in our proposal. It would save an enormous piling-up of debt which posterity will have to pay.
The other day a speech was made by an hon. member which was later dealt with by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), and to which I wish to refer indirectly. I have great regard for the hon. member who made that speech. I heard him speak in this house a few years ago in support of the textile workers of this country, and listening to his speech of the other evening and reading it afterwards, I came to the definite conclusion that what had inspired his speech was not a want of patriotism but rather fear-fear of financial disaster, fear of bankruptcy following this war. That is what we are threatened with and what we were threatened with even before the war started, and I believe that that fear has had a very bad effect upon our war effort. Because of it men have hesitated to enlarge
their operations as they otherwise might have done. As you go through the country people will tell you in a guarded way that they are frightened and nervous as to the consequences of this war because of the tremendous debt which will be piled up. I believe that that fear should be removed. Let me read a short extract from the address made by the president of one of our chartered banks at their annual meeting. He said:
Generations following us will labour under the burden of debt now being accumulated. There is but one remedy-drastic economy, a greater production, a greater foreign trade.
I notice that he does not mention greater consumption. He goes on:
We must reduce the number of governments and end the scandal of erecting luxurious public buildings. We must revise the franchise so that the unfit and unworthy do not have equal rights with those who work and produce and pay. We believe in liberty of press and speech, but licence to agitate cannot be tolerated. Let us hope the way to these reforms will be made clear at the coming dominion-provincial conference.
It is that sort of thing which has made people nervous, and one cannot wonder at it, when they are threatened with bankruptcy as a consequence of winning the war. I would ask members this question: If we lose the war, there will be no question of bankruptcy because Hitler will put his bailiff in and the country will be under his orders. But we are not going to lose the war. We are going to win the war. Everybody knows that. Then who is going to make the country bankrupt? Who has the power to make this country bankrupt except another and a greater power? An individual is made bankrupt by the court which orders the sale of his assets. The bailiff enters his home or place of business and his goods are sold. But who is to put a nation through that process? The idea presupposes a power which is greater than the sovereign government; and unless we lose the war, who can be superior to the sovereign power of this parliament-unless in the meantime we surrender our sovereignty?
Just in that connection let me say that there is a movement under way in Canada at the present time-groups are being formed all over the country and we hear the idea expounded over the radio and read it in pamphlets and literature distributed-which has for its object the surrender of the sovereignty of this country. I have brought this to the attention of the Minister of Justice before, and I wish to do so again because it seems to me a traitorous movement. At this time, during the confusion of
The Budget-Mr. Jagues

the war, when, people's minds are wholly taken up with fighting these German gangsters and going all-out to do so, here are these people, mostly from a country which so far has not taken any part in the fighting, spreading through fear the idea that the only thing to save the world is the destruction of nationhood, that the only way to avoid war is for every country to surrender its sovereignty to an international control which will have control over the armed forces, over finance, over fiscal policy and even over the judiciary. I should like to know what sovereignty would be left. That movement is known by some people as "federal union" and in this country as "union now". I believe it is the most subversive movement in the country to-day. It is based on the idea of the concentration of power, not in any one country, but a world concentration of power-the very thing we are fighting against. That is just what Hitler wants, and it is what he will have if he can get it. Yet there are people working night and day trying to persuade people that when we win the war we should surrender our sovereignty-that is, our ability and our power to control ourselves according to our own desires and wishes-to an international control over which we would have no say whatsoever.
So far as post-war conditions are concerned, unless finance takes over control as it did after the last war, there is no reason at all for any depression, and no reason-indeed, no possibility-of bankruptcy. I am the last to advocate that any individual should profit as a result of the war, but there is no question that as a result of the war our powers to produce will be immensely increased. Think of the hundreds of thousands of men who will have learned a skilled trade during the war. Think of the immense increase in machinery. There is no question that the powers of production in this country will be immensely increased. There is no question that, given a real financial system which works for the benefit of the country and not for the benefit of the financial system, we can be rewarded, as we should be, for winning the war, by a very great and general raising of the standard of living. Those Jeremiahs and croakers who say that as a result of winning the war we shall have to put on sackcloth and ashes, that we shall have to tighten our belts, are Hitler's best agents, the most dangerous fifth columnists we have. The man who gets up at the street corner on a soap-box and talks the old-time

red socialism and communism has little influence on the public; but when you threaten the living standards of the people, when their pockets are threatened, when the men who control the financial system of this country tell them that as a result of this war we shall be bankrupt and everybody will have to accept a much lower standard of living, we have a most dangerous brand of propaganda, and one which should be stopped at all costs.
I shall say only a few words with regard to agriculture, for the subject has been thoroughly aired in this house during the session. I agree with those who have said that agriculture has been badly used by this government, and I concur in the suggestion of various organizations that the price of seventy cents is totally inadequate and should be raised. That could be done quite easily by use of the Bank of Canada credit; and if the government cannot control inflation it is not a government, it is nothing but a tool of the financial interests. Inflation can be* controlled; and if it is not controlled, it is proof that the government is not a government.
In conclusion I want to renew my opposition to the proposal, of which we have heard much in certain quarters, for the surrendering of our sovereignty, or what amounts to the selling out of the British empire. Who is it that is fighting to save the world, or democracy, or freedom, and even Christianity? Who but the British empire? Is there anybody else doing it? Greece very gallantly did what she could, but now, beside the British empire-

speechtext: The Chinese.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, that may be so, but it could hardly be said that they are fighting for Christianity.

speechtext: Oh, yes; their leader is a Christian.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yet it is suggested that the sovereignty of the British empire should be surrendered and the control transferred into the hands of those who so far have not risked a little finger to save the world from anything. One remark I read in a pamphlet devoted to this propaganda was to this effect, that "even if England is beaten, all is not lost; we shall then have the use of the British fleet". Let me tell the writer of that article that, so long as the British fleet is above the water, Great Britain can never be beaten, and that if England is beaten, her

The Budget-Mr. Wright
fleet will be at the bottom of the sea and not on this side of the Atlantic. I believe that the British empire, with all its faults, is the greatest hope for the freedom of the world.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The only hope.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then, why tolerate a campaign which would sell it out? If another nation likes to come within this empire as a sovereign state, under the same conditions that Canada and Australia are in the commonwealth, owing a common allegiance to the crown, I am all for it. But when people demand that every state of the British empire should surrender its sovereignty and resign itself to an international control, I say that such an idea should be considered as traitorous and not tolerated in time of war.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak at this time it is my intention to confine myself chiefly to two subjects: first, the interests of the men in the army and their dependents; and, second, the effect of the budget and the regulations which we have passed in this house upon agriculture in the country as a whole.
Before speaking on these subjects, however, I should like to say that I fully realize the tremendous task with which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) was faced in bringing down the budget at this time; in particular, the tremendous expenditures which he has to find money to meet. I believe that he has conscientiously endeavoured to spread the taxation over as wide a field as possible, but I cannot agree with hon. members who have said he has done it on as equitable a basis as it could possibly have been done. For instance, the man with a $700 income, who under the old budget was paying $14, is paying, under this budget, $35, an increase of approximately 120 per cent; the man with a $50,000 income has also had his taxation increased, but to the extent of only fifteen or twenty per cent. I believe that current taxation should be based not so much upon the amount of income paid, as upon the amount which the man has left to spend after he has paid his taxes.
Many sections of the press and some members of the house have described this as a pay-as-you-go budget, but how many members *would consider themselves on a pay-as-you-go basis if they were spending approximately forty per cent more than their incomes and were compelled to raise that amount each year by borrowing? So far as I can see, we are financing this war on practically the same basis as we financed the last war; that is, we are taxing to the extent that we deem it 14873-174
politically expedient to do so, and we are raising the rest of the money by borrowing, on bonds bearing interest at whatever rate we think we can get them sold for. This is what was done during the last war and it is being done to-day. True, a larger proportion is being raised by way of taxation than in the last war. That is largely due to the fact that, after almost fifteen years of Liberal administration since the last war, the people of Canada have become more tax conscious than before. For their education in this line we must give the government credit.
We are going to be raising this year by taxation a sum larger than we raised during any two years in the last war. The interest we are going to pay is not as large as in the last war, but the amount of carrying charges will be larger, and it is this interest which we shall have to pay on all this debt that will be the greatest problem for us after the war is over.
It does not appear to me that it matters so much how much we owe if all this money we owe is owed to ourselves. If we owe it to ourselves as a result of borrowing it entirely within the country, we are borrowing it from ourselves, and after the war we shall be paying interest back to ourselves. If this money were borrowed from all sections and all classes of the people on an equal basis, it would not matter so much. But is that going to take place? I do not think so. How much of the loan that we shall raise during the coming summer will the farmers be able to subscribe to after ten years of depression and at present prices of agricultural products? And they constitute thirty per cent of the population-people just as loyal as any other section of the community. They will not have the money to subscribe to this loan. Then we have the men in our armed forces. At their rate of pay, and with their dependents, how much will they be able to subscribe? They are doing well if they can take a few wTar savings certificates. Then we have another large class of the population, unmarried men with a salary of $900 and less and married men with a salary of $1,500 and less. Just how much of the loan will they be able to subscribe? Not a very large amount. Already they are buying war savings certificates.
These three classes constitute seventy per cent of the population of Canada, and they will be unable, even if they wished to do so, to subscribe to any large extent to the loan that will be floated. This means that the other thirty per cent will have to subscribe approximately seventy per cent of the loan. After the war is over, how shall we pay the interest on the loan? All sections of the country, the farmers and the men from overseas, will be

The Budget-Mr. Wright

asked to pay their share of interest on it, and that is why we in the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation believe that these loans should be raised free of interest. Those classes who are unable to subscribe their share, no matter how much they may wish to do so, will be asked in future years to pay interest in perpetuity on this money. We are still paying interest on the money raised in the last war, and we shall be paying interest in perpetuity on the money raised for this war.
We believe that our chartered banks should be nationalized and that the Bank of Canada should be used to a far greater extent than it is to-day in the financing of this war. We might just as well try to stop a modern German panzer division with the machine guns and barbed wire used in the last war as try to finance this war, with its immense cost, by the same methods as were used at that time. If wre are to be successful, we must adopt some other method. I do not think that at this time we are using to the best advantage the financial, material or human resources of Canada.
The government is following the policy which it did in peace time; it is going only as fast as it is pushed by the people. That may have been a good enough peace-time policy; it may have been good enough political strategy, but it is a poor policy on which to fight and expect to win an all-out war. We should have conscription of the financial and material resources of the country for an allout war.
We know that there is on deposit in the savings banks one and a half billions, hundreds of these accounts consisting of $20,000 and more. Why should the government not have the use of this money for the duration of the war? If the farmers are asked to produce the necessities of life without profit, or even at a loss; if the working people are being asked to give their labour at a mere living wage, and sometimes not even that, then I say that these accumulations of unused capital, which is not being used to-day for some definite war purpose, capital accumulated out of the exploitation of the natural resources and labour of the common people of the country, should be taken advantage of.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? He speaks of accounts of $20,000 which he says the government could easily levy upon. What would be the minimum account on which he suggests the government would be entitled to levy?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Savings accounts of S20.000 or over, accumulations of capital which are not being used to-day for any definite war

purpose. There is probably close to one billion dollars of accounts in the banks. I forget the exact figures; they were given last year in the house. We are not making full use of the material resources of the country at this time. We are using for peace-time pursuits and pleasures many things that could be used for a fuller war effort. I have travelled over this country from one end to the other, and I see no one curtailment of pleasures; people are travelling as usual, buying as many cars as usual and doing the same as they did before, apparently without any idea that it is necessary for them to make sacrifices to win the war.
We have been told by many ministers that anything which is physically possible and desirable can be made financially possible for the winning of the war. We have in western Canada thousands of tons of scrap metal; we have unused rolling stock on our railways; we have railway men who are being employed part time; we have a department of wrar services, and yet they have not been able to devise any scheme to collect this metal and place it where it is needed in Canada. That is not using the material resources of the country as fully as they could be used.
We are not using the human resources of this country to the best advantage. We say that we need trained mechanics, yet in garages from one end of this dominion to the other we have thousands of trained mechanics who are servicing your car and mine so that we may go on a week-end trip, or play golf at our favourite golf club. It seems to me that these men should be used for a better purpose to-day.
The government has placed a small tax on gasoline. I suppose that is being done for several reasons: in order to secure revenue; to stop the use of gasoline for pleasure purposes, and, of course, to conserve the necessary foreign exchange. Strange to say, however, the same tax is placed on the gasoline used by a farmer to produce the food that we must have, that is placed on the gasoline used by a man driving out to his club for a game of golf. That does not seem fair, by any means. I believe that some distinction should have been made in this regard.
After having listened to discussions on agriculture in this house for the better part of two sessions; after having studied the legislation and regulations brought down with regard to agriculture, my advice to the Canadian farmer would be to join his local cooperative association, his local farm organization, and try to develop them into dominion-wide organizations that will do something for the farmers, because if they depend upon this

The Budget-Mr. Wright
government as it is presently constituted, certainly they will go to bed hungry. We must learn to do things for ourselves. Since the war started, whenever the price of an agricultural product has come anywhere near the cost of production, that price has been promptly pegged by the government. Long before the price of wool reached the cost of production, the government pegged that price. Last year, when the price of butter was getting somewhere near the cost of production, that price was pegged, with what result? Just the other day I was reading the statistics with regard to the exports of dairy cattle to the United States, which show that during the first three months of this year those exports increased by thirty-five per cent, and this at a time when we need all our dairy cattle to produce the cheese for which Britain is asking. That increased export of dairy cattle was due largely to the fact that butter prices were pegged last winter. The farmers came to the conclusion that, with wages rising and prices pegged, they could not afford to hire labour or buy machinery to milk their cows, and they disposed of their cattle while there was a good market for them in the United States. As a result, we shall have a shortage of butter in this country before another year is over, if we produce the amount of cheese that will be necessary in order to meet Britain's requirements.
I do not know whether it was the intention of the government, but in imposing a tax on gasoline used for agricultural purposes they are really handing a plum to the manufacturers and operators of certain types of engines used for agricultural purposes in Canada to-day. The man with a diesel tractor will not have to pay the tax, nor will the man who uses distillate. Who are the men using this type of fuel? They are the large operators, the mortgage companies, who own large tracts of land. They are the only people who can carry the overhead involved in the use of diesel machinery, but they will not be required to pay this tax. The man operating a smaller farm, using a high compression engine-and this will include the great majority of the farmers of western Canada-will have to pay this additional tax.
The other matter with which I wish to deal has to do with soldiers and their dependents. Just a short time ago there were brought to my attention several cases concerning soldiers' dependents who had the misfortunate to suffer serious illnesses which required their confinement in hospitals for considerable periods of time. The hospitals were unable to collect from these people; they had not the money with which to pay their bills. At this time I believe the government
14873-174J
should institute some health insurance scheme for soldiers' dependents, to take care of the cost of hospitalization and medical care. It is absolutely impossible for a soldier's wife with two children, receiving perhaps $79 a month, to build up a reserve to provide for any serious illness that may occur. The case of a soldier's mother, receiving $35 or $40 a month, is even worse. If these people suffer a serious illness, it means that they must go in debt. I know that the medical profession and the hospitals of this country will see that they are given the necessary care, but I do not believe these people should have to go in debt for the rest of their lives for this care. We should give our soldiers' dependents a better deal than that, and should institute some system of health insurance, which I believe should be contributory, to care for these people. I am sure they would be willing to contribute, in the case of a married man perhaps SI a month, and in the case of a single dependent, 50 cents a month. The government should assume responsibility for organizing this scheme and seeing that it is put into effect. It would give our soldiers a great deal more confidence if they knew their dependents would be looked after in case of serious illness.
This question of health insurance is something to which I believe we must pay more attention than we have done in the past. I know sixty per cent of the municipalities in my constituency have a municipal doctor employed to look after their people. Some of the .municipalities have free hospitalization, which is paid for by a general levy included in their taxes; and there is not one municipality that has had this system in force for any length of time that would want to return to the old method. The only trouble is that many of the municipalities cannot institute this scheme because they are not able to raise the necessary taxes. I know of one municipality that applied to the provincial government only last year for permission to develop a scheme of this kind, but the government replied that since the municipality had not been able to raise sufficient money to keep the schools open, the government could not see its way clear to grant the municipality permission to provide medical care. The reeve of that municipality in conversation with me said that in the municipality there were a great number of children who had defective eyesight and defective hearing, and who needed tonsil and adenoid operations and dental attention. It was his opinion that the municipality would be farther ahead if those children were given a sound body than if they were given only an education. He felt that if they could not have both, the building of a sound body should have precedence over the education.
The Budget-Mr. Wright

I say it is a disgrace to us in Canada to admit that there is a place in our country where we cannot give our children both a sound body and an education. I believe that, sooner or later, we must consider some form of medical health insurance. I am not going to enter into an argument to-night as to whether it should be municipally, provincially or federally controlled. In my opinion there is something to 'be said for each viewpoint. I believe, however, that if this government were to institute some scheme of health insurance for soldiers' dependents, it would give to us some valuable experience to follow after the war. We would learn something which would be invaluable to us later on in instituting a wider scheme.
I would urge the government, therefore, that it institute at this time some form of health insurance for soldiers' dependents. Speaking earlier in the house, I made reference to insurance for soldiers. In Canada, when the war broke out, the insurance companies inserted, in all new policies sold, a war clause whereby, in the event of an insured person being killed on active service, the beneficiary would receive only repayment of premiums paid. The companies also threatened to increase rates on policies, despite the big margin of safety provided by the present rates.
In contrast to this, when the selective service act in the United States was put into force in October, 1940, the trainees and all enlisted and commissioned officers in the United States army were offered insurance under a socialized scheme, known as national service insurance, at a rate far cheaper than it could be secured from private insurance companies. I should like to give hon. members an outline of that scheme in the United States, because I believe some such scheme might with good results be instituted in Canada.
No sales pressure was needed to put the idea across with the new recruits, who already have taken out more than S500,000,000 worth of new policies. The trainees are given four months to decide whether they want the insurance. They may take out policies to the amount of $10,000, which is the maximum under the scheme. The premiums may be deducted from the trainee's payroll, and after he leaves the service they are payable to the veterans administration in Washington. Rates are graduated according to the age at which the policy is taken out. At twenty-one years of age the monthly rate is sixty-five cents per. $1,000 of insurance; for a person thirty-four years of age the rate is seventy-five cents per $1,000.
Some conditions are attached to the policies. When first taken out, they are what is known
[Mr. Wright.l
as five-year term insurance. That is, the benefit is payable only in case of death within five years; and if the insured is still living at the end of that time, the policy expires automatically. But at the end of the first year the insured is given the option of converting this policy into one of the ordinary types of insurance policies; straight life, twenty-payment life, or thirty-payment life. Of course he pays a higher premium after conversion, because he is given much greater protection. But he has had from one to five years to think over whether he wants the insurance, and what kind he wants. If not, he has made only a few nominal payments, and so 'has not lost much. If he does want it he can obtain the type desired at a cheap rate and at the rate for the age at which he first subscribed. In other words, he has been able to take the insurance almost on approval.
This means a great deal to the lower-income groups. In the United States it has been found that about eighty-five per cent of the small policies paid for by weekly deductions from wages are either surrendered or allowed to lapse before a benefit is payable at either death or policy maturity. That is, a great many people buy insurance which gives them or their beneficiaries no benefit at all. Under the national service insurance there is no selling pressure, and so there should be less instances of persons buying insurance they do not w'ant. And the premiums are not weighted to provide a rake-off to build up assets and profits for a small management group of a private company.
We might very well institute in Canada some form of insurance for our soldiers which would give them some protection and give their dependents protection. It is said that we had soldiers' insurance during the last war, but I might point out that we did not have it during the war. After the war, a policy was made available to men who, because of injuries received in the war, could not qualify under regular insurance schemes.
Another thing which is taking place in the west-I do not know if it is taking place in the east-is that-

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Before the hon. member leaves that point, might I inquire if it is estimated that the scheme is self-supporting?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is, the government will not have to carry any burden?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The government is carrying all management charges, but is not making any profit out of the scheme.
Another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the house is connected with something which is occurring in Saskatchewan.

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
The dependents of soldiers are being taken off relief when they are receiving the deferred pay of the soldiers. That is, they are not receiving any pension but get only the deferred pay. One case has been brought to my attention. This has reference to a man sixty-nine years of age living in southern Saskatchewan in the municipality of White Valley. This man has been on relief for a number of years. They have not had a crop down there, and last year his crops were eaten by grasshoppers. Last year his wife died, and his married daughter, whose husband is serving overseas, came to live with him. Because she came to live with him he was taken off relief, and the municipality told him that because she was receiving soldiers' deferred pay and allowance she should be able to provide for him.
In my opinion that condition should not be permitted to continue. When a soldier is sending his deferred pay to his parents, I say it should be placed in trust for the reestablishment of the soldier after the war. That is the least that should be done. Certainly it should not be used as an excuse to cut his family off relief, nor should the family be forced to live on that money. Yet I know that that is the practice in Saskatchewan to-day. That is one of the methods used to take men off relief. I have in my hand a copy of the recommendation by the director of relief recommending that this man be cut off relief because his daughter is in receipt of an allowance from her husband who is serving overseas. That is the way in which we are treating our men in our fighting forces. Certainly I think we must give them a better deal. We are now going out to recruit more men for our forces. We need more men, and will continue to need more. If we want to get those men, then we must give the men in our army a decent deal.
With regard to the transportation of soldiers, I do not know that I need to go into this matter because it has been dealt with fully by many speakers. I fully agree with them when they say that our soldiers should receive their transportation. During the last session many hon. members in all parts of the house expressed their desire that this should be done, yet we find the government in this budget not only ignoring these requests but adding a further tax of ten per cent on these fares. I have met men coming from Valcartier and Debert camps going to the west on ten days' leave. This gives them only three days to spend at home, and it costs them anywhere from $50 to $100, depending upon whether they eat decent meals on the train and take a berth. It costs them from $2 to $3 for every hour they are able to spend
at home. I contend that men on their yearly furlough and last leave should have their transportation paid.
Speaking this afternoon, the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) dealt with the three points I have mentioned; the financing of the war, the position of agriculture during the war, and the treatment accorded the men in the armed forces. We who are in the opposition can say as much as we like about these matters, but we cannot put the pressure upon the government that private members on the government side can exert. It is their responsibility to see that this legislation goes through. We on this side of the house are willing to support them if they will put the necessary pressure upon the government. It is their responsibility to see that the men in the armed forces get a square deal, that agriculture is treated fairly and that this war is financed in a way which will not leave this country buried in debt after the conflict is over. I leave that with them.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak in this debate, but the other day the hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene) rose in his place, launched into an ecstatic flight of partisan rapture, and spent half an hour sowing seeds of suspicion, distrust and disunity. I think I should make an answer. He slandered and maligned with base misrepresentation, Mr. Aberhart, a great public-spirited and noble statesman.
There were many other problems which needed his attention. There was the gasoline tax which will prove absolutely ruinous to the province of Alberta which the hon. member has the honour to represent. This tax will prove injurious to the farmers who, in the main, make up his constituents, and it will prove injurious to the truck drivers upon whom they depend in a large measure for transportation. There is the sugar tax, which is almost a disaster to Alberta. There is the abolishing of relief which will hurt thousands in the province before we are finished. There is the agricultural policy of this government which is a tragic farce. There is the mounting debt that no one can see how we can ever repay. There is our present unemployment which is a reflection upon the government, and there is the threatened unemployment after the war which is likely to overwhelm the country. There is the question of our disappearing markets.
There was plenty for the hon. member to spend his time upon; he did not need to go dragging in provincial politics. There are plenty of dominion problems here to take care of. If there had been an election in the offing, it would have been different, but since
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

there is no election in the offing, the words of the Hon. member amounted practically to subversion of the government which is in power in Alberta. That government was returned by the people of Alberta after four years of successful operation, and that ought to entitle it to the respect of every person in the Dominion of Canada, no matter who he is or what he thinks.
An indication of the sort of thing we were going to have to listen to appeared early in his speech when the hon. member referred to the splendid young man who is the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw). I think this hon. member gave one of the most constructive, advantageous and profitable speeches heard in this house. During the course of his remarks he happened to refer to the pioneers, and at page 2653 of Hansard the hon. member for Athabaska broke forth with these words:
It amazes me to hear him speak of pioneering in the west and refer to the terrible treatment of the pioneers by this government. With reference to the hon. member's use of the word "pioneer", it is with pride that I say that fifty years ago last fall I had the honour, as a little boy, to become a settler of the great province of Alberta. I ask him, as a friend of Alberta, to leave this word alone in the future.
Upon what conceivable grounds can the hon. member ask the hon. member for Red Deer to leave the word "pioneer" alone? If the hon. member for Athabaska had taken the trouble to inform himself as he seems to think he is informed op everything, he would have learned that the father of the hon. member for Red Deer is a Nova Scotian who moved to southern Alberta near the United States boundary in 1885. He was employed by a Hudson's Bay Company trading post and ranched there for twenty-five years. He was in the Alberta provincial police for fifteen, years as a stock inspector and detective. I ask whether or not such a record does not give his son the right to speak of pioneers? His mother is of United Empire Loyalist stock, and she went to Alberta in 1899 to teach school. She is somewhat of a pioneer herself. The hon. member for Red Deer was born in Alberta in 1909. Although he did not come quite "as early as the hon. member for Athabaska, he did his very best to come as soon as possible. He is one of the seventh generation on his father's side and fifth generation on his mother's side born in Canada. He is related to two fathers of confederation, namely, Tilley and Tupper. He taught school in one of the oldest settled parts of Alberta for eleven years and lived right among the pioneers. During most of his speech he

advocated old age pensions, and the hon. member for Athabaska knew full well that he was unable to answer his arguments.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Is the hon. member going
to leave it without dealing with the grandparents of the hon. member?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I could deal with
the grandparents if the hon. member wishes me to. If he knew what was coming, he might not want me to continue. The remarks of the hon. member for Athabaska about pioneers reminds me of a story about the Dey of Alexandria. It is said that the British sent a squadron to deal with the Dey of Alexandria for misdemeanours on the high seas, piracy toward British ships. It happened that the young man in charge of the British squadron was exceedingly youthful looking. When he appeared before the Dey of Alexandria, the latter said, "I am surprised at the Queen of England's audacity to send a beardless boy to deal with me." The young man said, "Had the Queen of England known that wisdom was measured by the length of the beard, she might have sent your deyship a he-goat." It would seem that the people of Athabaska measured wisdom by the length of the beard when they sent their present member to parliament. They got a man to represent them who was apparently unable or unwilling or indisposed to get the facts in several important directions.
I am going to quote, as evidence, from page 2655 of Hansard-.
I would like hon. members of the Social Credit party to tell the Premier of Alberta that he has not been pulling his weight in this war. The province of Alberta has not yet done one solitary thing to help this government in carrying on the war. So far as I have been able to ascertain it has not offered to the government a single building to be used for war purposes.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, might I
interject with your permission? The hon. member for Athabaska (Mr. Dechene) is not at present in the chamber. There was a mistake made. He either said or intended to say "with the exception of providing a building or buildings." He meant to make that correction to-day, and probably will make it to-morrow. He meant to say, not "So far as I have been able to ascertain it has not offered to the government a single building," but that the province had offered some buildings to the government.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I accept the explanation of the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw), and I appreciate it. I am anxious to give the hon. member for Athabaska all the benefit of the doubt, and so I

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
accept my hon. friend's explanation. Personally I did not hear him. I assure the hon. member that it is rather spoiling the enjoyment I am getting out of making this speech to find that the hon. member for Athabaska is not in his seat. Again, may I assure the hon. membei for Medicine Hat that I accept his explanation?
May I now read' the statement issued by Premier Aberhart from Edmonton? Before I do so, may I draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the downright shame it is to make it necessary for the premier of a province of this dominion to defend himself against attacks which are uncalled for?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And scurrilous?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They are scurrilous.
May I read Premier Aberhart's statement? He said:
I was astounded and very much disappointed to learn that Mr. Dechene, the representative for the Athabaska district, should be so disloyal to his own province as to make such untrue statements and create such a false impression in his unwarranted attack on Alberta during Thursday's debate.
I could not understand how ministers of the crown could allow his statements to go uncor-reeted when he said that we had given no buildings to the federal government for war purposes.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is now reading a statement which, if the hon. member were to make it himself, would not be allowed in the house. Much less can statements that are contained in a communication from someone outside the house be read here. The hon. gentleman cannot quote a statement, from one outside the house as against a member of the house.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker, and I will simply summarize the facts, without using the actual words, which are contained in the statement. It is pointed out in this statement that the Edmonton normal school, the university dormitories and the Edmonton exhibition buildings have been placed at the disposal of the commonwealth air training plan. The Calgary normal school, the institute of technology and art, the Cam-rose normal school, and the Vermilion school of agriculture have also been given over gladly to the dominion government, and the public works department of the province has granted the dominion government the use of its machinery-a point with which I shall deal more fully a little later on. I am sorry that the whole statement cannot be read. It is unfortunate. Your ruling, Mr. Speaker, shows how helpless a man is, even one who occupies the position of premier of one of the provinces of this dominion, when a member of this house maliciously attacks him; for
your ruling makes it impossible for a member to defend the premier by reading his statement to the house.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Let him defend himself in Alberta.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It just shows how
careful a man ought to be before he attacks a man in the high position of premiership of one of the provinces of this dominion.
I have learned this, that there was $100,000 worth of machinery of the public works department of Alberta turned over to the dominion government without cost, without charge, voluntarily, to be used in the construction of airports, aerodromes, and other important public works in connection with the war effort. In Grande Prairie, the province of Alberta even sent its own personnel to work, I am told, crushing materials, surveying, and in various other ways contributing to the construction of the airport. I understand that there is a big Jaeger paver, worth S26,000 at work on various projects. Then there are huge machines, mixers, bulldozers and caterpillars, worth tens of thousands of dollars, which have been lent freely to the dominion government. There are 600,000 acres of land in the Tilley East district which, I am told, were offered to the dominion government at SI for ninety-nine years to be used in connection with war work.
It is difficult, Mr. Speaker, for a person to restrain himself under such circumstances as that. Are we to imagine for one minute that the hon. member for Athabaska could not learn that these things were true? Are we to suppose that he did not want to know? It is difficult to keep from suspecting that he did know and then disregarded the facts. What for? To sow the seeds of suspicion and distrust in this countiy in time of war simply because-well, what was the reason? Just because the people in charge in Alberta now do not call themselves Liberals, I suppose. But there are plenty of people in the government of Alberta now who were Liberals ten years ago.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They saw the errors of their ways and changed?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not know. I
am going to read two or three extracts from the last budget speech delivered in the legislative assembly of Alberta on March 10, 1941, and inasmuch as these quotations do not bear on this debate, Your Honour, I presume it is in order for me to read them. I read from a little pamphlet of the budget speech of the Hon. S. E. Low, delivered on March 10, 1941. At page 8, he says:
With respect to the advances made in the year 1937, under the guarantee of both the dominion government and the province, the arrangements provided that the banks would
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

carry the loans for a period of three years from the date the loan was made. I am glad to say, Mr. Speaker, that the province was in a position to take up the unpaid balance which totalled $519,098.13, and thereby relieved the dominion government of any liability under its guarantee. The amount outstanding on these loans, you will note, was since reduced to $452,532.60 as at December 31, 1940.
All those familiar with public affairs will readily appreciate how great was the service done there by the province of Alberta.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Did they not just do what any honest man ought to do?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Exactly, but it
seemed to me that the hon. member for Athabaska was trying to convey that they were not honest men.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, I do not think so.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I cannot tell, but it certainly looked that way. I read now from page 15 of Mr. Low's budget speech:
The figure shown for the dominion and provincial youth training programme ($78,975) is the net amount after deducting reimbursements from the dominion government. You will note that this activity has been extended to include a special course of training for war services. In Calgary the technical school has been turned over to the dominion authorities for training purposes, and other premises were secured by the province to carry on the technical schools. At Camrose, the normal school is being utilized by the military authorities and we are cooperating in every way

Note these words:
-and we are cooperating in every way possible with the dominion government in carrying on whatever training services they propose in this province.
I ask you. Mr. Speaker, how could the Alberta government do any more?
I turn now to page 17, and read:
Let me also add, Mr. Speaker, that this government is anxious and ready to cooperate with the dominion government and the other provinces of Canada in any undertaking which will render more effective and complete the Canadian war effort, to the end that the empire of which we form a part may be preserved and that man's free agency as embodied in democracy may not perish from the earth.
It is time that there was a secret understanding among the members of every party in this house that hereafter they will refrain from such malignant utterances as we listened to the other day, because they can do no possible good, and must do harm all over this country. I find myself disgusted with the whole situation. I cannot understand why it is that the mere fact that a man stops calling himself a Liberal or a Conservative

brands him as a disloyal member of the British commonwealth. I cannot see through that thing at all; it does not make sense, no matter how one looks at it.
I turn now to another matter on which the hon. member spent considerable time. As reported at page 2655 of Hansard, he referred to the textbooks of Alberta-as though the dominion legislature could have any conceivable interest in the textbooks that a province prescribes for its schools. The particular textbook under consideration was one used in grade nine in "social studies", a sort of history. It is a study of history, political economy and many other subjects which the people of our generation did not study in school, but which, I understand, they are studying all over Canada now; a good course, designed to give the young people some sort of understanding of the world in which they live. The textbook, according to the hon. member, was called "The World of To-day", which sounds like a sensible sort of textbook for young people to be studying. I have never been able to figure out why it was that the hon. member did not read from the text the passage upon which he based his remarks. He says:
In this book it is mentioned that there are three alternative systems of government to the present democratic system-communism as in Russia, C.C.F.-ism, and social credit.
I tried to get contact with the book so that I could read the passage into Hansard and hon. members themselves could study it. To me it is astonishing that the hon. member did not 'himself read it and allow hon. members to form their own opinions. But he made a statement concerning the passage, and allowed people all over the Dominion of Canada, who have no possible chance of gaining access to that text, to form a misconception of the things being done in the province of Alberta. I am sorry that the passage is not yet available. I asked the hon. member this afternoon, and he honestly tried to get it, but he had lent it to somebody and had not been able to get it back. That is too bad, is it not? I have a copy coming from Alberta which will be here to-morrow, but it is not here to-night, and the result is that the misrepresentation must continue.
He mentions that there are references to Russia, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and social credit. I would say that if the government had caused the book to be written, and if it had been anxious to promulgate the doctrines of social credit, it would have done what any ordinary group of men would have done-left Russia and the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation out and dealt only with social credit. As I recall the passage in question, all the teacher does who

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
wrote the textbook is to mention these three philosophies and ask the student if he can tell what each one stands for.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is the same text that was in Saskatchewan, where they have a Liberal government.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that right?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It has been used there.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is most interesting. I did not know it, but the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) says that it is the same text as that used in Saskatchewan, where there is a Liberal government.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They will have to take it out of Saskatchewan now.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I cannot vouch for the fact, but I assume that the hon. member knows, because he is a teacher in Saskatchewan.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A minister.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I gather that he knows. If it is true, how gross was the misconception conveyed to the people of Canada through that speech!

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the hon. member say that social credit or the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation creed, or both of them, are philosophies?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It depends largely upon what one calls a philosophy. We have not time to examine the meaning of the term. I have myself studied philosophy a good deal, but I do not know that it could be defined in a short time.
As to the educational system of Alberta, I take it that it is very much like the educational systems of most of the provinces in this dominion. It seeks to give the boys and girls the truth about all matters, and I myself would certainly be very much disappointed if a child of mine, after going through the ten or twelve grades of school, did not know something about what Russian communism is, what nazism is, what are the proposals of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, what Social Credit proposals are, and what Liberalism is.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What is it? What is Liberalism?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will not undertake to say. So I contend that the teacher, in giving boys and girls an understanding of the meaning of various expressions they hear used every day, is by no means doing anything unsound.
Even if the book were as bad as it is represented to be, in what way was Premier Aberhart responsible for it? It will be noticed that, while the debate was going on, while the hon. member's speech was progressing,
I asked him who wrote the book, because it was an important matter to know who wrote that book.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What book?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The book he was discussing.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who was the minister of education in Alberta at that time?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I asked who wrote the book, and, no matter who the minister of education was, that would have an important bearing on the matter, would it not?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who was the minister of education in Alberta at that time?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are coming to that in a minute or two. I asked who wrote the book, and there could be no reason why the hon. member should not tell me. He had the book in his hand.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that any reason for not telling us who was the minister of education in Alberta?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will very soon tell you. I presume you know.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, I know, and so do you. He is responsible, too.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You had better get your smartest questions, because I am ready for them. I asked who wrote the book, and the hon. member refused to tell. After I had asked four times, he said that my manners were bad.
