We will come to that in just a minute. I have a letter, Mr. Speaker, from Edmonton, dated May 10, bearing on this book. Of course we in this house could not be expected to know about it. How in the world can members of this house be expected to know everything about every textbook used in every course in the province of Alberta, who wrote it, and when, and who prescribed it, and when? It is impossible. If the hon. member for Athabaska did not know that, there is something seriously wrong with the hon. member. The letter is as follows:
Dear Mr. Blackmore:
I think you should have the facts with reference to our school text in social studies, authorized for use in grade IX.

There are some hon. members, from whom I never hear any other word with intelligence in it, who are always saying "order".
This book, entitled "The World of To-day" was prepared in 1936 by Gilbert Patterson, editor for the Ryerson Press, Toronto, and W. D. McDougall then principal of the normal practice school in Edmonton.
If that fact had come out in debate the other day, it would have avoided a whole lot of delusion.
The manuscript was submitted to the department's curriculum committee of which Doctor Newland is chairman. It was turned over to the sub-committee on social studies, composed of teachers and university men, and recommended for adoption. It was published in 1937 and used without criticism during the school years 1937-38 and 1938-39. After the outbreak of war it was felt that the book was too generous in its references to Germany and Russia. The minister thereupon appointed a special committee of persons entirely outside the department to examine the book and outline any revisions thought necessary. This committee submitted its report and the changes suggested were incorporated without alteration. The revised edition was then authorized to replace the original book and has been in use during the current school year.
It was not withdrawn in the way the hon. member said it was.
A copy of the revised book as now in use is going forward to you concurrently.
I trust this may give you the information you need to put Mr. Dechene straight.
Sincerely yours,
William Aberhart, Minister of Education.
The trouble is that there is just enough truth in the remarks made by the hon. member to make the statements dangerous falsehoods. The most dangerous lies in the world are half-truths. May I submit that in all probability the hon. member for Athabaska got himself elected by using just such propaganda as that throughout his constituency.

Next, the hon. member referred to the sabotaging or torpedoing of the Sirois report. He called my arguments rotten and suggested that I debate with him. He is not sufficiently experienced with me, or probably he would not have done that. I wonder whether he can debate. I wonder whether he ever stops talking long enough to let his opponent speak. I wonder whether he can really get the facts. I will undertake with the hon. member something most unusual; I will undertake to prove to him on any platform, if he will let me talk once in a while, that Mr. Aberhart did not torpedo the Sirois report; that Mr. Aberhart, Mr. Hepburn and Mr. Pattullo all objected to it, and that four other premiers definitely indicated that they would not be ready to accept the Sirois report as it stood.

If I had time enough I could prove that to the hilt. I have all the proof here. To hon. members who are so sure about the matter, I commend this little volume called "The Dominion-Provincial Conference," which contains every word of it. Those three premiers definitely objected to the report, and four others showed strong disinclination to accept it. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), I am afraid, will have to assume a good deal of responsibility for whatever happened to the report, whether you call it sabotaging or torpedoing.
I will give the reasons upon which I base my statement, and it might be well for the hon. member for Athabaska to be thinking about this so as to prepare himself for the discussion when the time comes.

The Budget

Mr. Blackmore
In the first place, the Prime Minister called the conference inopportunely. It was a wrong time to call it, and he knew it and said so himself. Then, when he sent out the letters calling the premiers from the provinces, he specified that they were to talk about the Sirois report only. There was no necessity for doing that. That meant that the conference was sure to fail if they did not feel like accepting the report. In the third place, he refused to discuss any other proposal. He asked that other proposals be given, and three of the premiers, two particularly, pointed out a new proposal. But it was disregarded. Finally, in the fourth place, the Prime Minister declared the conference closed. There was no declaration on the part of any of the provincial premiers that the conference was closed. The Prime Minister of Canada declared it closed.
If I am wrong in what I am about to say, I beg pardon, but the hon. member for Athabaska, I thought, reflected on the loyalty of the social credit organization as an organization. At least, that is the impression I gathered. I wish to read into Hansard an editorial published in the Edmonton Journal of January 18, 1936, which was written before this group ever came to parliament at all. It indicates clearly the stand which this group took on the first occasion on which it got together when all its members were newly elected:
The statement issued by Mr. Blackmore, the *leader of the Social Credit federal members, at the close of their recent caucus, hardly justifies the conclusions reached in a letter that is published to-day. There is no fascism about the party's policies as they were defined. They recognize that the preservation of peace and the defence of national interests require the maintenance of armed forces.
Up to that time not a single member or leader in the Dominion of Canada had had the courage to come out and say that-not one, until this little group did it.
The caucus also held that Canada must be prepared to do her part in providing these. No one should be open to the charge of holding fascist ideas because of taking such a position.
The increase of armaments that is in prospect is a most disappointing development to all who want to see the reign of law established in international affairs and an end put to war. But where the responsibility lies is quite clear. No matter how peace-loving a nation may be, it has to consider the conditions that exist in the world to-day and act accordingly. Britain has been exceedingly anxious to avoid adding to her armament burdens but in its present situation has no alternative. Nor can Canada be content with merely expressing the desire for peace.
Mr. Blackmore stated that his group favoured "such steps on Canada's part as will render her powerful enough in all respects to plan an effective part in any world crisis with which
the League of Nations might be called upon to deal." That was why expenditures on military, air and naval forces were urged. "Is it right or just?" the Social Credit leader asked, "that we should depend on Great Britain to defend us or on the United States?" Surely there can be only one answer to his question.
While it was contended that there should be more unity with the British commonwealth of nations and that we should do our fair share in strengthening the hands of the league, the opinion was expressed that much could be done toward eliminating the factors that lead to war. The claims of Italy and Japan for more territory in which to expand were sympathetically viewed. The need of economy changes which "would mitigate and ultimately remove completely the causes of war" were stressed. There is no doubt that the league can accomplish a great deal toward that end. It will have to grapple with these problems. But it requires from each of its member nations more than well wishes. For backing it up adequately, in ease its authority is challenged, they have to be prepared.
As the leader of the group that issued that statement, I think I can challenge any other leader in the dominion at that time and declare that he had never issued a statement as progressive or as far-seeing. That was the stand taken by this group. Does it or does it not show vision, courage and leadership?
When we came here we took a position along with the right hon. Prime Minister in support of greater armaments. We had some difficulty with some of our members who had not learned to see things as they have learned since to see them; but all the leaders of the group stood solidly behind the Prime Minister on that occasion, showing that they knew what it was all about. At that very time, however, some of the wordy and allwise members on the Liberal side were talking against a more intense war effort.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I think I have said enough. In conclusion, let me say that we came here this year and last year, with the country at war, firmly resolved that not a member of our group would say anything in the nature of low, cavilling political criticism. I challenge any hon. member on the government side to go through our speeches with a fine-tooth comb and find anything partaking of low, cavilling political talk. We believe in social credit; we believe in monetary reform. Like Mr. Aberhart at the conference on the Sirois report, we believe you will have to bring in monetary reform if you are going to bring the war to a successful conclusion. What contribution can we make in this house? Undoubtedly our best contribution is an advocacy of the principles of monetary reform ; and if we cease to advocate those principles, we cease to do the thing we were sent here to do. But the advocacy of the principle of monetary reform; the finding fault with the government's policy, as being an unwise policy, from a monetary point of view, certainly do not constitute cavilling criticism. We are simply putting our case squarely before the house in a straightforward manner.
It is not pleasant for me to- indulge in this sort of talk for forty minutes, Mr. Speaker, but I would point out that four or five hon. members on the government side have attacked us definitely in just this fashion; I thought it about time we showed we do not take things like that lying down.
